set_title: CLAT PG Practice Set 02 (Constitutional Amendments and Landmark Cases, Recent to Past; Trap-Annotated)

pattern.ordering: P01-P16 constitutional amendments with linked cases, arranged from recent to past; P17-P25 other subjects
pattern.note: Practice set, not a mock; original passages and questions (none taken from Mock 01-06 or Practice Set 01). The official paper has 120 questions in 120 minutes; this set is longer for extra practice.

instructions: Each question has four options and exactly one correct answer.
Correct answer carries 1 mark; each wrong answer carries -0.25.

Passages are original summaries for practice, current to mid-November 2026. Verify pending or evolving matters (e.g. the 131st Amendment Bill, the Sabarimala reference, the Delhi services Act challenge, BNS s.152 challenge) against current official sources.
Every explanation includes why the other options fail, the CLAT trap, and any language trick.

passages.title: Women's Reservation, Delimitation and the Amending Procedure: The 106th Amendment and the 131st Amendment Bill
passages.passage: The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, known as the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, inserted Articles 330A and 332A, reserving one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and in State Legislative Assemblies for women, including within the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The reservation extends to the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi but not to the Rajya Sabha or the Legislative Councils. It is to take effect only after a delimitation exercise that follows the first Census taken after the commencement of the Act, and it operates for fifteen years, which Parliament may extend. The allocation of seats among the States has been frozen on the basis of the 1971 Census, a freeze first imposed by the Forty-second Amendment and extended up to the first Census after 2026 by the Eighty-fourth Amendment, so that delimitation touches the political weight of States. Under Article 368(2), an amendment needs a majority of the total membership of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting; where the amendment seeks to change, among other things, the representation of States in Parliament, ratification by the legislatures of not less than half the States is also required. In April 2026, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill was introduced to bring the women's quota into force by 2029, to raise the ceiling on Lok Sabha seats from 543 to 850 and to carry out fresh delimitation on the basis of the 2011 Census. On 17 April 2026 the Lok Sabha voted 298 in favour and 230 against; since 352 votes were needed to reach the two-thirds mark, the Bill failed. Supporters argued that enlarging the House would let women be accommodated without displacing sitting members; critics warned that delimitation could alter the federal balance to the disadvantage of States that had stabilised their population growth. Whether and in what form the proposal returns should be verified against current parliamentary records.

questions.question: The 131st Amendment Bill failed in the Lok Sabha because

options.A: it was moved in the Lok Sabha, whereas a Bill to amend the Constitution must originate in the Rajya Sabha
options.B: it secured fewer than two-thirds of the members present and voting, though more members voted for it than against it
options.C: it did not obtain a majority of the total membership of the House, which is the only numerical test for an amendment bill
options.D: it had not been ratified by the legislatures of half the States before the Lok Sabha was asked to vote on it

questions.explanation: 298 members voted in favour and 230 against, so 528 were present and voting and two-thirds of that figure is 352. The Bill had a simple majority of those voting but fell short of the special majority.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is wrong because 298 is more than half of the 543 seats, and the total-membership test is only one of two tests. Option C is wrong because ratification, where needed, follows passage by both Houses. Option D is wrong because an amendment Bill may originate in either House.
questions.clat_trap: A simple majority of votes feels like victory, so the tempting error is to think 298 against 230 means the Bill passed. The trap is the double requirement in Article 368(2): total-membership majority AND two-thirds of those present and voting.
questions.language_trick: 'fewer than two-thirds ... even though more ... for than against' - the concessive clause is the true statement; the other options each assert a single test as the 'only' one.

questions.question: Suppose 30 of the 230 members who voted against the Bill had instead been absent, the other votes remaining as recorded. The Bill would then have

options.A: passed, because absent members are treated as having voted with the majority for counting the special majority
options.B: still failed, since two-thirds of the 498 members present and voting is 332 and 298 falls short of it
options.C: passed, because 298 would exceed two-thirds of the 498 members present and voting once fewer members opposed it
options.D: still failed, since 298 would not amount to a majority of the total membership of 543 in the House

questions.explanation: With 30 fewer opponents, 200 vote against, so 498 are present and voting. Two-thirds of 498 is 332. 298 is below 332, so the Bill still fails the two-thirds limb, although it clears the total-membership limb (272).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gets the arithmetic wrong: two-thirds of 498 is 332, not below 298. Option C wrongly says the total-membership test is unmet; the majority of 543 is 272 and 298 exceeds it. Option D invents a rule that absentees count with the majority; absentees are simply not counted.
questions.clat_trap: CLAT PG likes a small numerical twist on a stated rule. The trap is to reduce the opposition and conclude the Bill passes without recalculating the two-thirds threshold.
questions.language_trick: 'present and voting' - absentees drop out of the base, which lowers the threshold but not enough here.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about the 106th Amendment are correct on the passage?
I. It reserves one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for women, including seats reserved for SC and ST.
II. It extends to the Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils.
III. Its operation awaits a delimitation that follows the first Census after its commencement.
IV. It is a permanent reservation that cannot be extended or discontinued.

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III restate the passage. Statement II is false because the reservation does not reach the Rajya Sabha or Councils. Statement IV is false because the reservation runs for fifteen years, extendable by Parliament.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II contradicts the passage on the Houses covered, and statement IV contradicts the fifteen-year term, so any option containing either fails.
questions.clat_trap: Statement-combination items punish partial verification: three of four statements can look obviously right, and the one that is slightly off (permanence) is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'only' in the options forces exact matching; 'cannot be extended or discontinued' is an absolute that the passage contradicts.

questions.question: The passage suggests that ratification by half the State legislatures became a live issue for the 131st Bill most plausibly because

options.A: the Bill sought to extend the reservation to the Delhi Assembly, a Union Territory, whose status is protected by the proviso
options.B: a fresh allocation of seats and a larger House alter the weight of States in Parliament, which the proviso covers
options.C: the Bill proposed to lengthen the term of the reservation from fifteen years, which the proviso treats as a federal matter
options.D: every amendment to the Constitution must be ratified by half the States, irrespective of the subject matter it touches

questions.explanation: The passage ties ratification to a change in the representation of States in Parliament. Delimitation and a bigger House bear directly on how much each State counts.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is wrong because ratification is needed only for specified subjects. Option C is wrong because the Delhi Assembly was already covered by the 2023 Act and no proviso concerns it. Option D is wrong because the passage does not say the Bill changed the fifteen-year term, and duration is not a ratification subject.
questions.clat_trap: The tempting universal rule (ratification for all amendments) is a common misconception. The real rule is subject-specific.
questions.language_trick: 'irrespective of the subject matter' - a sweeping phrase that the passage's 'among other things, the representation of States' contradicts.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: The 106th Amendment itself fixed 2029 as the year from which the women's quota would operate
options.B: The women's quota under the 2023 amendment applies to the NCT of Delhi Legislative Assembly
options.C: The freeze on the allocation of seats among States traces to the Forty-second and Eighty-fourth Amendments
options.D: Critics of the 131st Bill feared that delimitation could disturb the balance between States

questions.explanation: The 2029 date belongs to the 2026 Bill, not the 2023 Act. The 2023 Act ties operation to delimitation after the first Census following its commencement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are each stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem plus a statement mixing the Act with the later Bill: the date 2029 is real, but attached to the wrong instrument.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT supported' - read each option against the text; 'itself fixed' shifts the date to the wrong enactment.

questions.question: As described in the passage, the legal position after 17 April 2026 is best stated as follows:

options.A: The 2023 Act stands suspended, because Parliament has shown that it cannot agree on the manner of delimitation and on the size of the House
options.B: The 131st Amendment has been enacted by Parliament, but its operation is deferred until the legislatures of half the States ratify it by resolution
options.C: The Lok Sabha's vote is a mere recommendation, and the Rajya Sabha may still pass the Bill so that it becomes law
options.D: The 131st Amendment Bill, having failed, has left the Constitution unchanged, and the 2023 Act operates only after delimitation

questions.explanation: A Bill that fails the special majority in one House does not become an amendment. The 2023 Act is untouched and its trigger remains delimitation after the first Census following commencement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats a defeated Bill as an enacted amendment awaiting ratification. Option B invents a suspension of the 2023 Act. Option C wrongly says a defeated Bill can pass through the other House alone.
questions.clat_trap: The trap is the difference between a Bill and an Act; students extend the 'women's reservation' headline to assume a change in law.
questions.language_trick: 'having failed' is the key participle; 'has left the Constitution unchanged' is the necessary consequence.

passages.title: Governors, Presidential Assent and the 2025 Reference: Articles 200, 201, 143 and 361
passages.passage: Article 200 provides that when a Bill passed by a State Legislature is presented to the Governor, the Governor may assent, withhold assent, or reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President and, where the Bill is not a Money Bill, may return it to the Legislature with a message for reconsideration. The Constitution prescribes no time limit. Article 201 governs the President's decision on a reserved Bill. In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor (8 April 2025), a two-judge Bench, invoking Article 142, read in a three-month outer limit and treated Bills as deemed to have received assent where the Governor had sat on them. The Union then made a reference under Article 143. In its opinion of 20 November 2025, a five-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice Gavai held that courts cannot impose timelines on the Governor or the President; that 'deemed assent' is unknown to the Constitution and cannot be created through Article 142, because that would substitute one constitutional authority for another; and that decisions under Articles 200 and 201 are not justiciable on their merits before a Bill becomes law. The Bench added that the personal immunity of the Governor under Article 361 survives but that the court may exercise limited review where inaction is prolonged, unexplained and indefinite, and threatens a constitutional standstill. It also noted that an advisory opinion under Article 143 is not adjudication of a dispute. Commentators have therefore asked whether the opinion displaces the April 2025 decision, which was a judgment in a dispute between parties, or merely departs from its reasoning. The question of the binding force of advisory opinions remains debated, and later developments should be verified.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a course open to a Governor under Article 200, as described in the passage?

options.A: Declaring the Bill void for want of legislative competence and returning it as an invalid enactment
options.B: Reserving the Bill for the consideration of the President
options.C: Returning a Bill that is not a Money Bill with a message for reconsideration
options.D: Withholding assent to the Bill presented by the State Legislature

questions.explanation: Article 200 offers assent, withholding, reservation, and (for non-money Bills) return with a message. The Governor has no power to declare a Bill void for lack of competence; that is for courts.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are courses expressly listed in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong-looking correct answer is the odd one out: students rush past a negative stem and select an option that seems to be a legitimate power.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT a course open' - negative stem; 'declaring void' sounds like a plausible gubernatorial check but is judicial.

questions.question: The 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejects 'deemed assent' principally because

options.A: the three-month outer limit in the April 2025 judgment had itself been held invalid by the opinion for that reason alone
options.B: assent under Article 200 is a legislative act, and legislative acts cannot be performed by deemed fiction under any circumstance
options.C: Article 142 cannot be used to let a Court take over a function entrusted to another constitutional authority
options.D: Article 361 gives the Governor absolute immunity, and so no inaction can ever be treated as consent

questions.explanation: The Bench reasoned from the separation of constitutional functions: Article 142 powers to do complete justice do not allow a Court to step into the shoes of the Governor or President.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the logic; the three-month limit is rejected because deemed assent is, not the other way round. Option B overstates Article 361 and contradicts the limited review the Bench preserved. Option D adds a general bar on legislative fictions that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: Option two is the seductive trap: Article 361 is mentioned, but the passage says personal immunity survives while limited review of prolonged inaction is available.
questions.language_trick: 'absolute immunity' and 'no inaction can ever' are absolutes; the passage keeps limited review.

questions.question: A Governor sits on a Bill passed by the State Legislature for eighteen months, giving no reasons and sending no message. On the 2025 opinion, the most defensible judicial response is

options.A: no remedy at all, since every decision under Article 200 is beyond judicial examination at every stage
options.B: limited review of the prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction, without fixing a deadline or declaring the Bill assented
options.C: a writ seeking damages from the Governor personally, since Article 361 does not cover inaction in the course of official duties
options.D: a direction fixing a three-month period and declaring the Bill to have been assented to on the expiry of that period

questions.explanation: The Bench left room for limited review of prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction but denied timelines and deemed assent. The Governor retains personal immunity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A describes the April 2025 approach, which the opinion declined to endorse. Option C ignores the limited review the Bench kept open. Option D contradicts the survival of personal immunity.
questions.clat_trap: The question tests the middle path: students oscillate between full judicial remedy (the 2025 judgment) and no remedy at all.
questions.language_trick: 'limited review' and 'without fixing a deadline' - the precise qualifiers matter; the wrong options each offer an all-or-nothing outcome.

questions.question: As regards the relationship between the April 2025 judgment and the November 2025 opinion, the passage best supports the view that

options.A: the opinion, being advisory, does not in form set aside the earlier judgment but departs from its reasoning, leaving its status debated
options.B: the earlier judgment was recalled by the same two-judge Bench on a review petition after the Union made its reference
options.C: the earlier judgment stands unaffected, because an opinion under Article 143 may never refer to or depart from an earlier decision of the Court
options.D: the opinion formally overruled the earlier judgment, because an opinion of a larger Bench is binding on all courts exactly like any decided case between parties

questions.explanation: The passage frames the question as open: a judgment in a lis is not formally set aside by an advisory opinion, but its reasoning is departed from, and the binding force of such opinions is debated.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states as settled what the passage calls debated. Option C invents a bar on referring to earlier decisions. Option D invents a review.
questions.clat_trap: Textbook trap of certainty: the passage itself says 'remains debated', so the options that settle the point either way are wrong.
questions.language_trick: 'merely departs' / 'remains debated' - hedged language signals an open question; absolute options like 'formally overruled' or 'unaffected' are not supported.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The Governor's immunity under Article 361 does not make prolonged inaction on a Bill wholly immune from judicial review.
Reason (R): The 2025 opinion held that Article 361 extends to the office of the Governor as well as to the person, so no court may examine any inaction under Article 200.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is supported: limited review of prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction is possible. R is false: the Bench held that the Governor's personal immunity survives, not that the office is shielded from all examination.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R contradicts A and the passage, so R cannot explain A and cannot be true.
questions.clat_trap: R sounds like the usual reading of Article 361, so students mark both as true or accept R as the explanation. The passage distinguishes personal immunity from the office.
questions.language_trick: 'extends to the office ... so no court may examine any inaction' - a clever repackaging of immunity into a total bar.

questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects the 2025 opinion on the justiciability of decisions under Articles 200 and 201?

options.A: Decisions under those Articles are justiciable on merits at all stages if the Governor has failed to give reasons for the decision
options.B: Before a Bill becomes law, the court cannot examine either the contents of the Bill or the merits of a decision under those Articles
options.C: A court may examine the merits of the Governor's decision, but not the Governor's inaction, before the Bill is enacted
options.D: A court may examine the contents of a Bill reserved for the President to decide whether it is constitutionally valid before assent

questions.explanation: Pre-enactment, the merits and the content of the Bill are beyond judicial scrutiny; only limited review of prolonged inaction is preserved.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A allows pre-enactment content review that the Bench denied. Option C adds a reasons-based exception not found in the passage. Option D reverses the position: merits are not reviewable but inaction is, in limited cases.
questions.clat_trap: Option three inverts merits and inaction, a classic reversal trap.
questions.language_trick: 'but not' and 'merits ... inaction' - the pairing is reversed in option three.

passages.title: GST and the Taxation of Mineral Rights: The 101st Amendment, Mohit Minerals and the 2024 Nine-Judge Decision
passages.passage: The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 introduced the Goods and Services Tax. It inserted Article 246A, giving Parliament and State Legislatures simultaneous power to make laws on goods and services tax; Article 269A, under which Parliament by law levies the integrated tax on inter-State supply; and Article 279A, which created the GST Council. It also narrowed Entry 54 of the State List and altered Entry 84 of the Union List. In Union of India v Mohit Minerals (2022), the Supreme Court held that the recommendations of the GST Council are persuasive and not binding on the Union and the States, because cooperative federalism contemplates dialogue and not command, and that both the Union and the States hold simultaneous power; it also held that integrated tax on ocean freight levied on an Indian importer could not stand. In Mineral Area Development Authority v Steel Authority of India (July 2024), a nine-judge Bench held by 8:1, with Nagarathna J dissenting, that royalty under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act is not a tax. The Bench held that Parliament's power under Entry 54 of the Union List to regulate mines and mineral development does not take away the States' power under Entry 50 of the State List to tax mineral rights, but that Parliament may, through its mining legislation, impose limitations on that power. A tax on land under the State List is a distinct subject. The Court allowed the States to claim dues from 1 April 2005, payable in instalments over twelve years beginning 1 April 2026, with no interest or penalty for the earlier period. The decision is often cited as a marker of fiscal federalism: the Constitution accommodates both a uniform national tax and a robust State authority over its mineral wealth.

questions.question: The effect of the Mohit Minerals decision on the GST Council's recommendations is that they are

options.A: binding on the States only, because the States have surrendered their power to levy goods and services tax to the Union
options.B: binding only where they have been adopted by a unanimous vote of the Union and all the State representatives
options.C: persuasive in character, reflecting cooperative federalism, and not binding on the Union or States as a matter of law
options.D: binding on the Union and the States alike, because the Council is a constitutional body created under Article 279A

questions.explanation: The Court read the Council's role as a forum for dialogue; its recommendations guide but do not bind, and Union and States retain simultaneous legislative power.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads constitutional status as binding force. Option B reads Article 246A as a surrender. Option D imports a unanimity rule that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: Because the Council is a constitutional body, students infer binding force. The trap separates institutional status from the binding quality of recommendations.
questions.language_trick: 'persuasive' vs 'binding' - the stem is directly about the quality of the recommendation.

questions.question: Under the 2024 decision, the State power to tax mineral rights is located in

options.A: Entry 54 of the Union List, since regulation of mines and mineral development is an exclusive power of Parliament
options.B: Entry 50 of the State List, subject to limits Parliament may impose by mining legislation
options.C: a tax on land under the State List, since mineral rights are inseparable from the land
options.D: Article 246A, since taxes on minerals are in substance taxes on goods and services

questions.explanation: The Bench placed the State's mineral-rights taxing power in Entry 50, subject to Parliament's limits, and distinguished the separate land tax entry.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A places the power in the Union List, which only regulates mines. Option C is wrong because the passage treats land tax as a distinct subject. Option D wrongly folds mineral rights into GST.
questions.clat_trap: The land-tax option is tempting because minerals are in the ground. The passage separates tax on land from tax on mineral rights.
questions.language_trick: 'Entry 54' appears in both Lists with different content - read the List named.

questions.question: A State levies a tax on mineral rights. The Union argues that royalty under the Mines and Minerals Act already occupies the field. On the passage, this argument is

options.A: sustainable, because the regulation of mines and mineral development lies wholly with the Union and leaves no field for the States
options.B: unsustainable, because Parliament cannot impose any limitation whatsoever on a State's taxing power under Entry 50
options.C: unsustainable, since royalty is not a tax and Parliament may impose limits without exhausting the State's power
options.D: sustainable, because royalty is itself a tax and two levies on the same mineral subject cannot co-exist under the constitutional scheme

questions.explanation: Royalty is not a tax, so there is no double taxation. Entry 54's regulatory power does not wipe out Entry 50, though Parliament can legislate limits.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A wrongly calls royalty a tax. Option B treats Union regulatory power as exhaustive. Option D is an overstatement: Parliament may impose limitations.
questions.clat_trap: Third option is the absolute-word trap ('any limitation whatsoever'), reversing the passage's qualification.
questions.language_trick: 'whatsoever' and 'cannot' - absolutes in a federal-balance question are suspect.

questions.question: Which statement about the Court's direction on past mineral-rights dues is INCORRECT?

options.A: Payment was to be made in instalments spread over a period of twelve years from the start date
options.B: The first instalment was to fall due from 1 April 2026
options.C: Interest was payable on the dues for the period before the decision
options.D: Claims could relate to a period beginning 1 April 2005

questions.explanation: The Bench gave relief: no interest or penalty for the earlier period.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option B and Option D accurately reflect the direction.
questions.clat_trap: Negative stem plus an option that sounds like a normal consequence of a tax default. The passage says the opposite.
questions.language_trick: 'INCORRECT' - the one statement contradicting the passage must be picked.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In the 2024 decision, the Supreme Court held that royalty under the Mines and Minerals Act is not a tax.
Reason (R): The 101st Amendment inserted Article 246A in the Constitution.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are true on the passage, but Article 246A concerns goods and services tax and has nothing to do with the classification of royalty.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is a true but unrelated fact; it does not explain the holding on royalty.
questions.clat_trap: Both statements come from the same passage and look related (taxation and the 101st Amendment), tempting students to mark the explanation option.
questions.language_trick: 'explanation' - test whether R actually supports A or merely sits near it.

questions.question: The passage uses 'Entry 54' for two different things. The correct understanding is that

options.A: Entry 54 of the Union List was narrowed by the 101st Amendment, while Entry 54 of the State List concerns regulation of mines and mineral development
options.B: Entry 54 of the Union List concerns regulation of mines, while Entry 54 of the State List was narrowed by the 101st Amendment
options.C: both references are to the State List, since the Union List does not deal with mines and mineral development
options.D: both references are to the same entry, whose scope was narrowed to enable State taxation of mineral rights

questions.explanation: Entry numbers repeat across Lists. The passage says the amendment narrowed Entry 54 of the State List and refers to Entry 54 of the Union List for mines.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A swaps the Lists. Option C merges two separate entries. Option D places the mines entry in the State List, which the passage denies.
questions.clat_trap: A purely linguistic trap: same number, different Lists. Many CLAT items hinge on reading which List is named.
questions.language_trick: 'Entry 54' - repeated numbering; the List name is the differentiator.

passages.title: The Forty-second Amendment and the Preamble: Balram Singh (2024), Minerva Mills and Tribunals
passages.passage: The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 made far-reaching changes. It inserted the words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' in the Preamble, added Part IVA containing fundamental duties under Article 51A, and introduced Articles 323A and 323B enabling tribunals. It also extended Article 31C, which the Twenty-fifth Amendment had first inserted to protect laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c), so that laws for any Directive Principle would be shielded from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, and it added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368 to bar judicial review of amendments. In Minerva Mills (1980), a Constitution Bench struck down the clauses added to Article 368 and, by 4:1, the extension of Article 31C, holding that the Constitution rests on a balance between fundamental rights and Directive Principles. In L Chandra Kumar (1997), the Court held that decisions of tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B remain subject to review by High Courts under Articles 226 and 227, because judicial review is a basic feature. The Preamble has long been the subject of controversy. In Berubari (1960), the Court said that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) rejected this view. On 25 November 2024, in Dr Balram Singh v Union of India, a two-judge Bench led by Chief Justice Khanna dismissed petitions challenging the 1976 insertions. It held that Parliament's power to amend extends to the Preamble, that the date of the Constitution's adoption on 26 November 1949 is no bar to later amendment, that 'socialist' signifies a commitment to a welfare State and does not forbid private enterprise, and that secularism, recognised as part of the basic structure in Bommai, is a continuing feature of the constitutional order.

questions.question: In Balram Singh (2024), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble

options.A: can be amended by Parliament, and the date of adoption does not prevent later amendments to it
options.B: can be amended only by a Constituent Assembly specially convened for the purpose by an Act of Parliament
options.C: can be amended only if the amendment is ratified by the legislatures of not less than half the States
options.D: cannot be amended at all, because it was adopted on 26 November 1949 as part of the original constitutional text and stands frozen

questions.explanation: The Court rejected the argument that the date of adoption bars amendment and confirmed Parliament's amending power over the Preamble.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is the very argument rejected. Option C and Option D invent special procedures not mentioned.
questions.clat_trap: A classic trap is to think the date on the Preamble freezes it in time. The Bench said otherwise.
questions.language_trick: 'cannot ... at all' - absolute; the passage supports the opposite.

questions.question: The view in Berubari (1960) that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution was

options.A: upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which treated the Preamble as a mere statement of aspiration and not part of the Constitution
options.B: upheld in Balram Singh (2024), which held that the Preamble cannot be amended for want of legislative competence
options.C: rejected in Minerva Mills (1980), which held the Preamble to be unamendable for it embodies the basic structure
options.D: rejected in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which accepted that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable

questions.explanation: The passage says Kesavananda rejected the Berubari view. Balram Singh then confirmed the power to amend.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the 1973 holding. Option B reverses the 2024 holding. Option C attributes to Minerva Mills a holding that is not in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Two cases and a reversal; the passage gives only one direction.
questions.language_trick: 'rejected' vs 'upheld' - verbs are reversed in the distractors.

questions.question: On the passage, the term 'socialist' in the Preamble signifies

options.A: State ownership of all means of production and a bar on private property
options.B: a commitment to a welfare State that is compatible with private enterprise
options.C: a constitutional mandate that all key industries be nationalised by the State
options.D: an equal distribution of income among all citizens by an annual redistribution

questions.explanation: The Bench read 'socialist' as a welfare-State goal that does not forbid private enterprise.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D are classical doctrinaire readings that the Bench did not adopt.
questions.clat_trap: Students carry the political-science meaning of socialism into a constitutional question. The Court's reading is functional.
questions.language_trick: 'does not forbid private enterprise' is the pivot of the correct reading.

questions.question: A State enacts a law to give effect to the Directive Principle on the right to work (a principle other than Article 39(b) and (c)) and claims immunity from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 through Article 31C. On the passage, the claim

options.A: succeeds, since Minerva Mills struck down Article 31C only in respect of the Directive Principles in Article 39(b) and (c)
options.B: fails, since Article 31C has been wholly invalid since Minerva Mills and no law can claim its protection
options.C: succeeds, since the Forty-second Amendment extended Article 31C to all Directive Principles and that extension remains in force today
options.D: fails, since the extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles was struck down in Minerva Mills

questions.explanation: Minerva Mills struck down the extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles; the narrower original protection (Articles 39(b) and (c)) survives.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the decision. Option B reverses which part was struck down. Option C says Article 31C is wholly invalid, which the passage does not support.
questions.clat_trap: The distinction between the 25th Amendment's narrow Article 31C and the 42nd Amendment's expanded version is the whole question.
questions.language_trick: 'only the narrower protection survives' - the precise remaining scope is in the correct option.

questions.question: According to L Chandra Kumar, the decisions of tribunals set up under Articles 323A and 323B

options.A: cannot be examined by High Courts unless the tribunal has itself declared a statute unconstitutional
options.B: can be challenged only before the Supreme Court, since the jurisdiction of High Courts over such tribunals stands ousted
options.C: are not open to any judicial review, since the tribunals are constitutional bodies equal in status to High Courts
options.D: remain open to review by High Courts under Articles 226 and 227, because judicial review is a basic feature of the Constitution

questions.explanation: The Court held tribunal decisions remain subject to High Court review under Articles 226 and 227.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A says High Court jurisdiction is ousted. Option B denies review altogether. Option C adds a condition not in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The 42nd Amendment sought to oust courts; Chandra Kumar restored review. The trap is the option that follows the amendment's intention.
questions.language_trick: 'ousted', 'not open to any' - signals of a legislative attempt to exclude review.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about the Forty-second Amendment and its judicial treatment are correct?
I. Parliament's power to amend extends to the Preamble.
II. The date of adoption of the Constitution is a bar to amending the Preamble.
III. Secularism is part of the basic structure, as recognised in Bommai.
IV. The clauses added to Article 368 by the amendment survived Minerva Mills.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I and III only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III follow from the passage. II is the argument rejected in Balram Singh and IV is false because Minerva Mills struck down the clauses.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: II and IV each contradict the passage, so any option including either is wrong.
questions.clat_trap: Four statements with two traps that reverse the Court's actual holdings; the trap is to recall the earlier case (Minerva Mills) only for Article 31C.
questions.language_trick: 'survived' vs 'struck down' - reversal on the Article 368 clauses.

passages.title: Reservation: The 103rd Amendment (EWS), Indra Sawhney and Sub-classification in Davinder Singh
passages.passage: The Constitution (103rd Amendment) Act, 2019 inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6), enabling the State to make special provisions, including reservation of up to ten per cent, for economically weaker sections other than the socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. In Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India (November 2022), a five-judge Bench upheld the amendment by 3:2. The majority, comprising Maheshwari, Trivedi and Pardiwala JJ, held that economic criteria alone are a permissible basis for reservation, that the EWS quota is a separate category which does not alter the basic structure, and that the fifty per cent ceiling laid down in Indra Sawhney (1992, nine judges) is not inviolable for such a separate category. Bhat J, with Chief Justice Lalit, dissented, holding that the exclusion of the poor among the SC, ST and OBC from the EWS benefit offends the equality code. In Indra Sawhney, the Court had also required exclusion of the creamy layer among backward classes and barred reservation in promotions; the latter was met by the 77th Amendment, which inserted Article 16(4A). In Davinder Singh v State of Punjab (August 2024), a seven-judge Bench held, by 6:1, with Bela Trivedi J dissenting, that sub-classification within the Scheduled Castes is permissible on the basis of empirical data showing inadequate representation, and overruled E V Chinnaiah (2004), which had treated the Scheduled Castes as a homogeneous class. Some judges in separate opinions suggested that the creamy layer principle might be extended to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; these remarks were not part of the Court's holding on sub-classification. The decisions illustrate a movement from caste-only toward data-driven and multi-criterion reservation policy.

questions.question: The majority in Janhit Abhiyan upheld the 103rd Amendment principally on the reasoning that

options.A: the fifty per cent ceiling of Indra Sawhney was itself declared unconstitutional and therefore inapplicable to any category
options.B: economic criteria alone are permissible and the EWS quota, a separate category, leaves the basic structure intact
options.C: economic backwardness is the foundation of the equality code, and caste can never be used as a criterion for any reservation
options.D: the exclusion of SC, ST and OBC poor from the EWS benefit is justified because those classes are already adequately represented in public services and education

questions.explanation: The majority treated EWS reservation as a separate category and said the ceiling is not inviolable for it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overstates: caste was not rejected as a criterion. Option C wrongly says Indra Sawhney's ceiling was struck down for all categories. Option D gives a reason the majority did not adopt.
questions.clat_trap: The ceiling point is limited to the EWS category; any option extending it universally is a trap.
questions.language_trick: 'separate category' - the qualifier the majority used.

questions.question: The dissent of Bhat J (with the Chief Justice) in Janhit Abhiyan rested on the view that

options.A: the 103rd Amendment had not been passed by the special majority required under Article 368(2) of the Constitution
options.B: reservation on economic criteria alone can never be a permissible basis, whatever the category of persons concerned
options.C: the fifty per cent ceiling in Indra Sawhney can be crossed only after a constitutional amendment ratified by the States
options.D: excluding the poor among SC, ST and OBC from the EWS benefit violates the equality code

questions.explanation: The dissenters objected to the exclusion of SC/ST/OBC poor, not to economic criteria as such.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is wrong because the dissent did not reject economic criteria in general. Option B and Option C are not stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Students expect the dissent to reject economic reservation altogether; the passage shows that it rejected the exclusionary clause.
questions.language_trick: 'excluding ... violates' - the object is the exclusion.

questions.question: A State, after collecting quantifiable data showing that one sub-group within the Scheduled Castes is grossly under-represented, earmarks a share of the SC quota for that sub-group. On the passage, this measure is

options.A: permissible even without any data, since sub-classification is a matter of legislative wisdom beyond judicial review
options.B: permissible in principle, since sub-classification on empirical data is allowed and Chinnaiah stands overruled
options.C: impermissible, since the Scheduled Castes form a homogeneous class, as held in Chinnaiah, which remains good law and binds the State until a larger Bench decides otherwise
options.D: permissible only for Scheduled Tribes, since the Davinder Singh decision does not extend to Scheduled Castes

questions.explanation: Davinder Singh held sub-classification permissible on empirical data of inadequate representation and overruled Chinnaiah.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A relies on an overruled case. Option C drops the empirical-data requirement. Option D wrongly confines the holding to Scheduled Tribes.
questions.clat_trap: The empirical-data condition is the exam hook. Without data the measure would not be supportable.
questions.language_trick: 'collecting quantifiable data' in the stem is what makes the correct option correct.

questions.question: The observations in Davinder Singh about extending the creamy layer to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are best described as

options.A: a binding holding of the Bench, by a majority of 6:1, requiring every State to exclude the creamy layer from SC and ST quotas
options.B: remarks of some judges in separate opinions, not part of the holding on sub-classification, and so not binding as a rule
options.C: an overruling of Indra Sawhney, which had confined the creamy layer principle to the Other Backward Classes
options.D: a holding binding on the Union alone, since the observations were made only on the reservation policy of the Central Government

questions.explanation: The passage says the remarks were not part of the Court's holding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns an observation into a ratio. Option C invents a Union-only binding effect. Option D wrongly says Indra Sawhney was overruled.
questions.clat_trap: Ratio versus obiter, with the 6:1 figure used as a lure in the first option.
questions.language_trick: 'were not part of the Court's holding' - a negative marker that kills the 'binding' options.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The EWS majority in Janhit Abhiyan held that the fifty per cent ceiling of Indra Sawhney is inviolable for every category of reservation.
Reason (R): The EWS quota is a separate category which operates outside the existing reservation for the SEBC, SC and ST.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false: the majority held the ceiling not inviolable for the separate EWS category. R is true on the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A contradicts the passage, so options that treat A as true fail.
questions.clat_trap: R is true and sounds connected to A, but it supports the opposite conclusion (the ceiling does not bind the separate category).
questions.language_trick: 'inviolable for every category' - an absolute that the majority did not hold.

questions.question: Which pairing of case and majority line-up is accurate on the passage?

options.A: Janhit Abhiyan was decided by 4:1 upholding the amendment, and Davinder Singh unanimously permitting sub-classification
options.B: Janhit Abhiyan and Davinder Singh were both decided unanimously, upholding the amendment and permitting sub-classification
options.C: Janhit Abhiyan was decided by 3:2 upholding the amendment, and Davinder Singh by 6:1 permitting sub-classification
options.D: Janhit Abhiyan was decided by 3:2 striking down the amendment, and Davinder Singh by 6:1 refusing sub-classification

questions.explanation: The passage states 3:2 for Janhit Abhiyan and 6:1 for Davinder Singh, with the dissenters named.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A misstates the split in both cases. Option B reverses the outcomes. Option D makes both unanimous.
questions.clat_trap: Bench arithmetic and outcome reversal in options that use the same numbers.
questions.language_trick: Numbers and verbs together: 'upholding' vs 'striking down'.

passages.title: Article 21 Widened: Privacy, Aadhaar, Climate and Data Protection
passages.passage: The Supreme Court's Article 21 jurisprudence has steadily widened the meaning of life and personal liberty. In K S Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017), a nine-judge Bench unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms in Part III. The Bench overruled M P Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent that those decisions had denied such a right, and the plurality condemned the majority reasoning in ADM Jabalpur. Restrictions on privacy must pass a four-part test: there must be a law, it must serve a legitimate aim, the means must be proportionate to that aim, and procedural safeguards against abuse must exist. Applying this framework in the Aadhaar case (2018), a Constitution Bench by a 4:1 majority upheld the scheme for welfare benefits under Section 7, but struck down Section 57, which allowed private entities to demand authentication, and read down the mandatory linking of Aadhaar with bank accounts and mobile connections. The majority also accepted the passage of the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill, with Chandrachud J dissenting. A related question, whether the Finance Act 2017 tribunal provisions could validly be passed as a Money Bill, was referred to a larger Bench in Roger Mathew (2019); its current status should be verified. In M K Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024), a case about the Great Indian Bustard, the Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change, reading it into Articles 14 and 21. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 now regulates the processing of digital personal data through consent, duties of data fiduciaries and a Data Protection Board, but exempts State instrumentalities on notified grounds such as sovereignty and public order. Critics argue that these exemptions, together with the changed personal-information exemption in the Right to Information Act, may weaken the proportionality safeguards laid down in Puttaswamy.

questions.question: According to the passage, in M K Ranjitsinh the Court located the right against adverse effects of climate change in

options.A: Articles 14 and 21, read as part of the right to equality and the right to life
options.B: Article 48A of the Directive Principles alone, enforced directly as a fundamental right
options.C: Article 51A(g) as a fundamental duty that generates a corresponding enforceable right
options.D: Article 19(1)(g) as a freedom of trade that is limited by environmental protection

questions.explanation: The passage states that the right was read into Articles 14 and 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B converts a Directive Principle into a right on its own, which the passage does not say. Option C treats a duty as the source of a right. Option D relocates the right to a trade freedom.
questions.clat_trap: Environmental rights are commonly tied to Article 48A and Article 51A(g), which makes the wrong options feel familiar; the question tests what the passage actually says.
questions.language_trick: 'read into' signals judicial interpretation of existing Articles, not a new Article.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: The nine-judge Bench in Puttaswamy decided unanimously that privacy is a fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution
options.B: The Aadhaar majority struck down Section 7 for welfare benefits while sustaining Section 57 for private use
options.C: The Data Protection Act exempts State instrumentalities on notified grounds such as public order and the security of the State
options.D: The Aadhaar Act's passage as a Money Bill was accepted by a majority of four judges to one, with one judge dissenting

questions.explanation: The passage says the reverse: Section 7 was upheld and Section 57 was struck down. The other statements are directly stated.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D each restate the passage correctly, so they cannot be the answer to a NOT question.
questions.clat_trap: The stem asks for the unsupported statement, and the unsupported option is a clean reversal of the holding, which looks natural to a student who skims.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT supported' inverts the usual task; the reversal of Section 7 and Section 57 is the trap.

questions.question: A State law authorises its police to collect biometric data of all residents for crime prevention, with no limit on retention and no independent oversight. Under the four-part test described, the law is most vulnerable because it

options.A: is invalid merely because it touches a Part III right, without any further test of its justification being applied
options.B: offends Article 21 only if the data is actually misused against an identifiable person who comes forward to challenge it
options.C: fails the first limb, since crime prevention can never be treated as a legitimate aim in a case that concerns privacy
options.D: lacks procedural safeguards against abuse and is probably disproportionate, even if its aim is legitimate

questions.explanation: The aim of crime prevention is legitimate. The weakness lies in the third and fourth limbs: unlimited retention is disproportionate and there is no oversight.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A wrongly treats crime prevention as an illegitimate aim. Option B ignores the structured test altogether. Option C requires actual harm, whereas the test examines the design of the law.
questions.clat_trap: A student may jump to illegitimate aim or to 'any intrusion is invalid'. The test asks which limb fails, and the answer lies in safeguards and proportionality.
questions.language_trick: 'even if' concedes the aim, which shifts the attack to the means.

questions.question: A private lender collects an applicant's phone number and uses it for marketing without consent. As described in the passage, which legal framework most directly governs the conduct?

options.A: The Right to Information Act, which regulates personal data held by private lenders
options.B: The Aadhaar Act, which lets private entities demand authentication from residents
options.C: The exemptions for State instrumentalities, which apply to any entity serving a public purpose
options.D: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which regulates processing through consent and duties of data fiduciaries

questions.explanation: The Act regulates processing of digital personal data by data fiduciaries and rests on consent. The lender is not a State instrumentality.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A refers to a provision that the Court struck down. Option B concerns public authorities, not private lenders. Option C stretches the State exemption to private entities.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'private' tempts students toward Aadhaar's Section 57, which was struck down.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Aadhaar judgment shows that a measure can satisfy part of the privacy test and still be partly invalidated. Reason (R): The Court sustained Section 7 for welfare benefits but invalidated Section 57, which allowed private entities to demand authentication.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are consistent with the passage. The partial survival of the scheme is exactly what the Reason describes.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: The Reason supplies the concrete split between the valid Section 7 and the invalid Section 57, which is the basis of the Assertion.
questions.clat_trap: Students sometimes treat a 4:1 upholding as a complete validation of Aadhaar, and so doubt the Assertion.
questions.language_trick: 'partly' in the Assertion is the cue to look for a split outcome.

questions.question: The reference to Roger Mathew (2019) in the passage is intended to show that

options.A: a larger Bench has already held that the Speaker's Money Bill certification is never reviewable
options.B: the Money Bill question left open in Aadhaar resurfaced in another statute and went to a larger Bench
options.C: the Finance Act 2017 tribunal provisions were struck down for want of legislative competence on that very ground
options.D: the Aadhaar majority's Money Bill holding was overruled by a larger Bench in that decision itself

questions.explanation: The passage says only that the issue was referred to a larger Bench, and advises verifying its status.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A claims an overruling that never occurred. Option C attributes a decision on the merits that the passage does not report. Option D states a final holding where there is only a reference.
questions.clat_trap: A reference is not a decision. Options that announce a result use certainty that the passage does not support.
questions.language_trick: 'referred' versus 'held': the verb decides the answer.

passages.title: Defection and the Tenth Schedule: 52nd and 91st Amendments, Kihoto to Subhash Desai
passages.passage: The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985), disqualifies a legislator who voluntarily gives up membership of the political party on whose ticket he was elected, or who votes against a party direction without condonation. In Kihoto Hollohan (1992), a Constitution Bench upheld the Schedule by a 3:2 majority but struck down paragraph 7, which barred courts from examining disqualification matters, because that change affected the High Courts and the Supreme Court and had not been ratified by half of the States under the proviso to Article 368(2). The Speaker, acting under the Schedule, was held to function as a tribunal whose decisions are subject to judicial review; courts would ordinarily wait for the final decision, interfering earlier only in exceptional, jurisdictional cases. The 91st Amendment (2003) deleted the earlier exception for a split of one-third of a legislature party, so that only a merger, supported by two-thirds of the members of the legislature party, is protected under paragraph 4. It also capped the Council of Ministers at fifteen per cent of the House. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020), the Court observed that a Speaker should ordinarily decide disqualification petitions within three months and suggested that Parliament consider an independent tribunal, because the Speaker belongs to a political party. In Subhash Desai (2023), a five-judge Bench held that the Speaker must recognise the whip appointed by the political party, not the whip chosen by the legislature party. It held that the Governor's call for a floor test, without objective material showing that the government had lost its majority, was not justified. However, because the Chief Minister had resigned without facing the floor test, the Court could not restore the earlier government. The questions on the powers of a Speaker who faces a pending removal notice, decided in Nabam Rebia (2016), were left to a larger Bench; their status should be verified.

questions.question: In Kihoto Hollohan, paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule was struck down because

options.A: it gave the Speaker an unfettered power which violated the freedom of speech and expression of legislators
options.B: it permitted disqualification for conduct not recognised as a ground of disqualification in Article 102 or Article 191
options.C: it affected the jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court without ratification by half of the States
options.D: it required the Speaker to decide within a time limit that the Constitution does not permit

questions.explanation: Paragraph 7 ousted judicial review. Since that affected the courts, ratification under Article 368(2) was needed, and it was missing.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a free-speech ground. Option B concerns the content of grounds, not paragraph 7. Option D confuses paragraph 7 with the Speaker's time of decision.
questions.clat_trap: A student recalls that Kihoto 'upheld' the Schedule and misses that the ouster paragraph alone was invalid for a procedural reason.
questions.language_trick: 'because' asks for the reason, not the result.

questions.question: Which of the following changes were made by the 91st Amendment (2003)? I. It deleted the exception for a split of one-third of a legislature party. II. It capped the Council of Ministers at fifteen per cent of the House. III. It introduced the Tenth Schedule into the Constitution.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I and III only
options.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: The 91st Amendment removed the split exception and capped the ministry. The Tenth Schedule came from the 52nd Amendment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement III attributes to the 91st Amendment what the 52nd Amendment did, so any option containing it fails.
questions.clat_trap: Amendment numbers invite swapping. Statement III is true of the Tenth Schedule but wrong as to its source.
questions.language_trick: The sentence 'introduced into the Constitution' sounds like a general fact, but the question asks about the 91st.

questions.question: The Speaker must recognise, as the whip, the person appointed by the political party. In a case where a legislature party elects a new whip while the party organisation has appointed a different one, the Speaker, following Subhash Desai, should recognise

options.A: the whip chosen by the majority of the legislature party
options.B: no whip, until the Election Commission rules on which faction is the party
options.C: the whip appointed by the political party
options.D: the whip of the faction that has the Speaker's support in the House

questions.explanation: The Court held that the whip is the party's, not the legislature party's.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the position that the Court rejected. Option B makes the Speaker's preference decisive. Option D adds an Election Commission step that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The majority-in-the-House option seems natural in a parliamentary system, which is why it is the main distractor.
questions.language_trick: 'political party' versus 'legislature party' is the exact distinction in the holding.

questions.question: The Court in Subhash Desai declined to restore the previous government because

options.A: the Tenth Schedule bars courts from restoring any government after a floor test has been called by the Governor
options.B: the Governor's decision to call a floor test was found to be justified on the material that was before him at the time
options.C: the Chief Minister had resigned without facing a floor test, so the earlier position could not be restored
options.D: the Speaker's disqualification order against the rebel members had already been upheld by the Supreme Court in separate proceedings

questions.explanation: The Court found the floor test call unjustified, yet resignation before the test prevented restoration.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the passage, which calls the floor test call unjustified. Option B adds an event that did not occur. Option D invents a bar in the Tenth Schedule.
questions.clat_trap: Students assume that a wrong Governor's act must lead to restoration. The passage separates the wrong from the remedy.
questions.language_trick: 'However' in the passage flags the exception to the usual remedy.

questions.question: The suggestion in Keisham Meghachandra that Parliament consider an independent tribunal rests mainly on the concern that

options.A: the Election Commission lacks any power to decide defection matters
options.B: paragraph 7 still bars courts from reviewing the decisions of the Speaker
options.C: the Tenth Schedule disqualifies members on grounds that Article 102 does not recognise, creating an inconsistency
options.D: the Speaker, being a party member, may delay or politicise disqualification decisions

questions.explanation: The passage links the suggestion to the Speaker's party affiliation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B state propositions the passage does not support, and the second contradicts Kihoto. Option C is a distractor with no basis in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The tribunal suggestion sounds like a response to a legal defect in the Schedule, whereas it responds to institutional bias.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: In a legislature party of thirty members, twelve members announce a separate group and join another party. After the 91st Amendment, these members are

options.A: protected, since paragraph 4 requires only a simple majority of the legislature party to approve a merger
options.B: protected only if the Speaker certifies the split to be genuine and based on a matter of principle
options.C: not protected by any split exception, and liable to disqualification unless twenty members accept a merger
options.D: protected, since twelve exceeds one-third of the strength of the legislature party and amounts to a valid split as the Schedule stood before the amendment

questions.explanation: The split exception was deleted. Only a merger backed by two-thirds (twenty of thirty) is protected.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies the deleted one-third rule. Option B invents a certification by the Speaker. Option D misstates the merger threshold.
questions.clat_trap: The number twelve is calculated to exceed one-third of thirty, which lures students who remember the pre-2003 rule.
questions.language_trick: 'After the 91st Amendment' sets the time frame; arithmetic then gives two-thirds of thirty as twenty.

passages.title: Free Speech and the Amendments to Article 19(2): From the First Amendment to Kaushal Kishor
passages.passage: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, subject to restrictions permitted by Article 19(2). The First Amendment (1951) was enacted after decisions such as Romesh Thappar and Brij Bhushan struck down press-related restrictions; it added 'public order', 'friendly relations with foreign States' and 'incitement to an offence' as grounds, and inserted the word 'reasonable' before 'restrictions', which made the restrictions open to judicial scrutiny. The same Amendment introduced Article 15(4) and Articles 31A and 31B with the Ninth Schedule. The Sixteenth Amendment (1963) added 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act as vague and capable of chilling speech, upheld the blocking power in Section 69A because it carries procedural safeguards, and read down the intermediary provision in Section 79. It distinguished mere discussion or advocacy from incitement. In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Court held that orders suspending internet services must satisfy proportionality, be published, be temporary and be open to review. In Kaushal Kishor (2023), a Constitution Bench held by a 4:1 majority that the grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive, so that no additional restriction can be imposed on the speech of public functionaries; that Articles 19 and 21 can, in some cases, be enforced against non-State actors; and that the State is not vicariously liable for a minister's statement made in a personal capacity. Nagarathna J agreed that Article 19(2) is exhaustive but wrote separately: she held that hate speech by public functionaries harms the dignity and equality of others, that Parliament may regulate it, and that a statement may be attributed to the government when it reflects the government's stance.

questions.question: The Sixteenth Amendment (1963) is linked in the passage to

options.A: the withdrawal of Ninth Schedule protection from laws affecting freedom of speech
options.B: the insertion of the word 'reasonable' before 'restrictions' in Article 19(2) of the Constitution
options.C: the addition of 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground of restriction
options.D: the insertion of 'public order' as a ground of restriction on freedom of speech

questions.explanation: The Sixteenth Amendment added sovereignty and integrity of India. Public order and 'reasonable' came with the First Amendment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B are First Amendment changes. Option D invents a withdrawal of Ninth Schedule protection.
questions.clat_trap: Two correct changes sit in the options, attributed to the wrong Amendment.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: According to the Kaushal Kishor majority, the grounds in Article 19(2) are

options.A: capable of being supplemented by executive guidelines framed by the Speaker
options.B: illustrative, so hate speech by public office-holders may be added as a further ground by the Court
options.C: applicable only to private citizens and not to Ministers or other public functionaries
options.D: exhaustive, so that no further restriction on speech can be read in

questions.explanation: The passage states that the grounds are exhaustive.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is closer to the dissenting concern and contradicts the majority. Option B invents an exemption for Ministers. Option C creates an executive route that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The sympathetic policy argument for adding hate speech pulls students toward the first option.
questions.language_trick: 'exhaustive' versus 'illustrative'.

questions.question: A Minister makes a derogatory remark about a crime victim in a personal capacity, and the remark does not reflect any stand of the government. Under the majority view in the passage, the State

options.A: is liable only if the remark is made after the Minister has taken the oath of office
options.B: is vicariously liable, since a Minister acts as the agent of the State at all times and in every capacity he holds
options.C: is not vicariously liable, though other remedies against the Minister personally may survive
options.D: is liable only if the Council of Ministers had collectively approved the remark

questions.explanation: The majority held that the State is not vicariously liable for a personal-capacity statement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the rule that was rejected. Option B adds an irrelevant condition. Option D adds a collective-approval condition not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The fact that the remark 'does not reflect any stand of the government' cuts off Nagarathna J's attribution route, so the majority position applies directly.
questions.language_trick: 'personal capacity' is the key phrase.

questions.question: An authority suspends internet services in a district by an unpublished order with no stated end date. Applying Anuradha Bhasin as described, the order is

options.A: valid, since the right to internet access is not part of any freedom guaranteed under Article 19
options.B: valid, as the executive's assessment of public order cannot be examined by a court
options.C: invalid only if the suspension is also shown to violate Article 21 and the person affected has first exhausted every remedy
options.D: open to challenge, since such orders must be published, temporary and proportionate, and reviewable

questions.explanation: The case requires publication, temporariness, proportionality and review.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the passage. Option B grants an unreviewable discretion. Option C imposes an extra condition that the passage does not state.
questions.clat_trap: Deference to security assessments is a tempting trap; the passage requires reviewability.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Shreya Singhal, Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was struck down but Section 69A was upheld. Reason (R): The Court struck down Section 79 of the Information Technology Act in its entirety as an unreasonable restriction.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Assertion is correct. The Reason is false, because Section 79 was read down, not struck down entirely.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: The Reason misstates the treatment of Section 79 and so cannot explain the Assertion.
questions.clat_trap: The three sections of the Act appear together, and the Reason is plausible because one of them was struck down.
questions.language_trick: 'in its entirety' is the false element; the passage says 'read down'.

questions.question: The separate opinion of Nagarathna J in Kaushal Kishor is best described as

options.A: holding that Article 19(2) is merely illustrative and that courts may add further grounds of restriction when needed
options.B: denying that Articles 19 and 21 can ever be enforced against any non-State actor
options.C: holding that every statement by a Minister, even one made on a government matter, always creates vicarious liability for the State
options.D: accepting that Article 19(2) is exhaustive, yet holding that hate speech harms others' rights and Parliament may regulate it

questions.explanation: She agreed on exhaustiveness but wrote on hate speech, parliamentary regulation and attribution to the government.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses her agreement on exhaustiveness. Option B uses 'always', whereas she required attribution to the government's stance. Option C contradicts the horizontal-application holding.
questions.clat_trap: A separate opinion is often misread as a complete dissent, which tempts students to reverse every point.
questions.language_trick: 'agreed ... but wrote separately' is a signal of partial divergence.

passages.title: Delhi and the 69th Amendment: Federalism Between the Elected Government and the Lieutenant Governor
passages.passage: The 69th Amendment (1991) inserted Articles 239AA and 239AB, giving Delhi the status of the National Capital Territory with a Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers. The Assembly may legislate on matters in the State and Concurrent Lists, except public order, police and land. Under the proviso to Article 239AA(4), if the Lieutenant Governor differs from the Council of Ministers on any matter, he may refer it to the President and act according to the decision. In State of NCT of Delhi v Union of India (2018), a five-judge Bench held that the Lieutenant Governor is bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except in matters referred under the proviso, and that 'any matter' means matters of an exceptional character and not every difference of opinion. In Government of NCT of Delhi v Union of India (May 2023), a five-judge Bench led by the Chief Justice held that the Delhi Government has legislative and executive power over 'services' under Entry 41 of the State List, excluding public order, police and land. The Bench relied on the 'triple chain of accountability': civil servants answer to ministers, ministers to the legislature and the legislature to the electorate. It reasoned that a government that cannot control its officers cannot be held answerable to the people. Soon afterwards, the Union issued an ordinance and enacted the Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, which created the National Capital Civil Service Authority. Parliament's power to legislate for the territory under Article 239AA(7) and the question whether it can nullify the basis of a judgment without overruling it have been referred to a larger Bench; the present status should be verified.

questions.question: The 69th Amendment (1991) is linked in the passage to

options.A: Articles 239AA and 239AB, which gave Delhi a Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers
options.B: Article 239A, which created a Legislative Assembly for the Union Territory of Puducherry
options.C: Article 371A, which created special provisions for the State of Nagaland
options.D: Article 240, which empowers the President to make regulations for Union Territories

questions.explanation: The passage attributes Articles 239AA and 239AB to the 69th Amendment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are real Articles on other Territories or States, and so are tempting but unconnected with Delhi.
questions.clat_trap: Familiar Article numbers in the options reward recall, not reading.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: In the 2018 decision, 'any matter' in the proviso to Article 239AA(4) was held to mean

options.A: every matter on which the Lieutenant Governor disagrees with the Council of Ministers
options.B: only matters relating to public order, police and land, which are outside the Assembly's power
options.C: matters on which the Assembly lacks legislative competence under the Constitution
options.D: matters of exceptional character, so that not every difference of opinion may be referred to the President

questions.explanation: The Bench read 'any matter' narrowly.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gives the Lieutenant Governor a blanket power. Option B confuses the proviso with the excluded subjects. Option C confuses it with legislative competence.
questions.clat_trap: The literal reading of 'any' favours the first option, while the Court read it down.
questions.language_trick: 'any' read as 'exceptional'.

questions.question: After the 2023 decision, the control of the Delhi Government over services is best stated as

options.A: excluded altogether, since Delhi is a Union Territory and all services belong to the Union Government
options.B: vested in the Lieutenant Governor, to be exercised in his discretion under the proviso to Article 239AA(4)
options.C: covering services under Entry 41 of the State List, except public order, police and land
options.D: extending to all services, including those connected with public order, police and land, without exception

questions.explanation: The Bench excluded only public order, police and land.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the three excluded subjects. Option B ignores that the Assembly has legislative power. Option D reintroduces the Lieutenant Governor's discretion which the Court limited.
questions.clat_trap: A student who remembers 'Delhi won' marks the broadest option.
questions.language_trick: 'except' in the correct option contains the limit.

questions.question: A civil servant in Delhi ignores a Minister's instructions on a matter of services. In light of the 'triple chain of accountability', this conduct

options.A: has no effect on accountability, since in matters of services civil servants answer to the Lieutenant Governor alone and to no one else
options.B: is the Union's concern only, since the Assembly has no power over any civil servant working in the capital
options.C: strengthens accountability, since the legislature itself answers to the civil service and to its senior officers
options.D: weakens the chain, because civil servants are meant to be answerable to Ministers, who answer to the legislature

questions.explanation: The chain runs from civil servants to ministers to the legislature to the electorate.
