questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the Court's reasoning. Option B inverts the chain. Option C ignores the holding that services fall in Entry 41.
questions.clat_trap: A hypothetical converts a doctrine into an application, and the wrong options look like administrative common sense.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The enactment of the 2023 Amendment Act after the judgment raises the question whether

options.A: the judgment automatically ceased to apply to every matter after the ordinance
options.B: Parliament can overrule a judgment by a simple declaration that it is void, as the sovereign legislature
options.C: Parliament can nullify the basis of a judgment by fresh law, without formally overruling it
options.D: the ordinance route is barred in the National Capital Territory

questions.explanation: The passage frames the issue as whether the basis of a judgment can be nullified without overruling it, and says it has been referred to a larger Bench.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states a legislative power that no court has accepted. Option B assumes the outcome. Option D is not stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The question tests the validation or override doctrine in a fresh setting, but only the framing is supported by the passage.
questions.language_trick: 'without overruling' captures the doctrine.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are correct on the basis of the passage? I. The Lieutenant Governor is bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers except in matters referred under the proviso. II. The Delhi Assembly may legislate on police. III. Entry 41 of the State List covers services, subject to specified exceptions.

options.A: I only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and III only
options.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Statements I and III are stated in the passage. Police is excluded from the Assembly's power.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II contradicts the exclusion of public order, police and land.
questions.clat_trap: Statement II is false by a single subject; students who recall that 'Delhi won' accept it.
questions.language_trick: The word 'police' sits among generally accepted powers.

passages.title: The 99th Amendment, NJAC and the Judges Cases: Appointments and Judicial Independence
passages.passage: Under Article 124(2), the President appoints a judge of the Supreme Court after consultation with such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as he deems necessary, and the Chief Justice of India is consulted in every case other than that of the Chief Justice himself. In S P Gupta (1981) the Court treated consultation as non-binding, giving primacy to the executive. In the Second Judges case (1993), a nine-judge Bench held that 'consultation' means concurrence, gave primacy to the Chief Justice's recommendation and created a collegium of the Chief Justice and the two senior-most judges. The Third Judges case (1998), an answer to a Presidential Reference, enlarged the collegium for the Supreme Court to the Chief Justice and four senior-most judges. The 99th Amendment (2014) inserted Articles 124A to 124C and created the National Judicial Appointments Commission, comprising the Chief Justice, two senior-most Supreme Court judges, the Union Law Minister and two eminent persons; any two members could veto a recommendation. In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (Fourth Judges case, 2015), a Constitution Bench held by 4:1 that the Amendment and the NJAC Act were unconstitutional, as the independence of the judiciary and the primacy of the judicial voice in appointments form part of the basic structure; Chelameswar J dissented. The collegium was revived and the Memorandum of Procedure was to be reconsidered. In Advocates Association Bengaluru (2023), the Court examined the delay and withholding of recommendations by the Government, reiterated earlier time limits (four weeks for the Intelligence Bureau's inputs and eight weeks for the Government's decision) and noted that where the collegium reiterates a name, the Government is bound to appoint.

questions.question: Which feature of the NJAC was most directly criticised as a threat to judicial independence in the passage?

options.A: The use of the word 'consultation' in Article 124(2) as it stood before the amendment came into force
options.B: The restriction of its functions to appointments to the Supreme Court alone, leaving High Courts to the collegium
options.C: The presence of the Chief Justice as a member of the commission, alongside two other senior judges
options.D: The power of any two members to veto a recommendation, blocking a name preferred by the judicial members

questions.explanation: The passage notes that any two members could veto a recommendation, so non-judicial members could block the judges' choice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the feature that favoured judicial voice. Option B is not stated in the passage. Option C describes a pre-amendment text.
questions.clat_trap: A student looks for the executive's presence alone and misses that the veto mechanism is the point.
questions.language_trick: 'veto' signals the operative device.

questions.question: Which pairing of case and principle is correct on the basis of the passage?

options.A: S P Gupta: primacy of the judiciary in appointments; Third Judges case: primacy of the executive over the collegium
options.B: Second Judges case: 'consultation' means concurrence, with primacy to the Chief Justice
options.C: Second Judges case: primacy of the executive in appointments to the higher judiciary; Fourth Judges case: a collegium of three
options.D: Third Judges case: the NJAC upheld as valid; Fourth Judges case: a collegium of five

questions.explanation: The Second Judges case read consultation as concurrence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses S P Gupta and misplaces the Third case. Option C reverses the Second case and misstates the Fourth. Option D invents holdings for both cases.
questions.clat_trap: Four cases with similar names invite shuffling of holdings and bench sizes.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The outcome of the Fourth Judges case, as stated in the passage, was that

options.A: the Amendment and the NJAC Act were struck down by 4:1 and the collegium system was revived
options.B: the Amendment was upheld but the NJAC Act was struck down by 3:2
options.C: the Amendment was struck down by 5:0 and the collegium was left to be reconstituted by Parliament
options.D: the Amendment and the Act were upheld by 4:1, with the collegium abolished

questions.explanation: The passage states 4:1, with Chelameswar J dissenting.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B splits the outcome and changes the ratio. Option C reverses the result. Option D changes the majority and the consequence.
questions.clat_trap: Ratios and consequences are altered in plausible ways.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: According to the passage, if the collegium reiterates a recommendation after the Government returns it, the Government is

options.A: bound to make the appointment
options.B: free to return it again for reconsideration on any ground
options.C: required to refer it to the Cabinet for a final decision
options.D: entitled to withhold it unless the President records satisfaction

questions.explanation: The 2023 Court noted that a reiterated name must be appointed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B allows an endless loop. Option C and Option D add steps not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The options use constitutional terms such as the President's satisfaction to seem authoritative.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Fourth Judges case restored executive primacy in judicial appointments. Reason (R): S P Gupta had treated consultation as non-binding and so given primacy to the executive.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Assertion is false because the Fourth Judges case revived the collegium and the judicial voice. The Reason is a true statement about S P Gupta.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: The Assertion reverses the result of the Fourth Judges case, while the Reason is accurate about an earlier case.
questions.clat_trap: The Reason is true and sounds related, which induces students to accept the Assertion on the basis of the earlier case.
questions.language_trick: A true Reason does not make a false Assertion true.

questions.question: The Government sits on a collegium recommendation for nine months without giving reasons. In light of the 2023 observations, this delay is

options.A: inconsistent with the time limits settled earlier, and the Court may monitor compliance
options.B: invalid only if the Chief Justice has first formally written to the Prime Minister about the delay
options.C: permissible, since the President's satisfaction on such recommendations cannot be examined by any court
options.D: permissible, since Article 124 itself prescribes no time limit for the President's decision on recommendations

questions.explanation: The Court reiterated four-week and eight-week time limits and examined delay.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B rests on the silence of Article 124 and ignores time limits laid down in judgments. Option C claims a non-justiciable satisfaction. Option D invents a formal precondition.
questions.clat_trap: Constitutional text without a time limit tempts students to conclude that no limit exists, ignoring judge-made limits.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

passages.title: The 97th Amendment, Cooperative Societies and the Ratification Requirement
passages.passage: The 97th Constitutional Amendment of 2011 gave constitutional status to cooperative societies. It added the words 'co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c), so that forming such societies became a fundamental right, inserted Article 43B as a Directive Principle on voluntary formation and democratic control, and created a new Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT). Part IXB lays down binding rules on the number and term of directors, reserved seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women on boards, supersession of boards and audit. Since 'cooperative societies' is Entry 32 of the State List, such controls over State cooperative societies curtailed the legislative power of State legislatures. The proviso to Article 368(2) requires that an amendment seeking to change certain federal matters, including the distribution of legislative powers in the Seventh Schedule, must also be ratified by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States. The 97th Amendment was passed by the special majority in Parliament but was not sent for such ratification. In Union of India v Rajendra N. Shah (July 2021), a Bench of three judges held by 2:1 that Part IXB is invalid to the extent that it applies to cooperative societies governed by State law, since the ratification demanded by the proviso was missing. The Court did not strike down the Part as a whole: it continues to operate for multi-state cooperative societies and for Union Territories, where it is Parliament that legislates. K.M. Joseph J., dissenting, would have upheld Part IXB entirely, treating its effect on State legislative power as incidental to protecting the associational freedom in Article 19(1)(c). The changes to Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43B were not challenged on the ground of ratification. The reasoning echoes Kihoto Hollohan (1992), where paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule was struck down for the same defect. A separate Ministry of Cooperation was created by the Centre in 2021; later legislative follow-up should be checked for current status.

questions.question: The majority in Rajendra N. Shah held Part IXB invalid for State cooperative societies because

options.A: the amendment curtailed a State subject without ratification by half the State legislatures
options.B: reservation of board seats for women and weaker sections offends Article 14 and the basic structure of the Constitution as a whole
options.C: Parliament lacks competence to amend a fundamental right such as Article 19(1)(c)
options.D: a Directive Principle cannot be added by amendment without a referendum in each State

questions.explanation: The defect was procedural and federal: Part IXB regulates a State List subject, so the proviso to Article 368(2) required ratification by half the States, which was not obtained.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is wrong because the Court did not question Parliament's power over Article 19(1)(c). Option C invents a referendum requirement that the Constitution does not contain. Option D attributes a substantive equality objection when the ground was procedural.
questions.clat_trap: Three options sound like constitutional grounds a student might know; the real ground is the unglamorous ratification proviso. The question tests whether you separate procedural from substantive invalidity.
questions.language_trick: 'Curtailed a State subject' hides the key link to Entry 32 of the State List.

questions.question: A multi-state cooperative society challenges the election-related provisions of Part IXB applicable to it, relying only on the missing ratification. On the passage, the challenge will most likely

options.A: succeed, since multi-state societies are also covered by Entry 32 of the State List and need ratification
options.B: fail, as the Court kept Part IXB operative for multi-state societies, over which Parliament legislates
options.C: succeed, since the Court held the whole of Part IXB void for want of ratification by the States
options.D: fail, since the dissent of Joseph J. is the binding view on the point

questions.explanation: The invalidity was limited to the operation on societies governed by State law. For multi-state societies and Union Territories the Part continues because the matter falls within Parliament's domain.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores that the Part was not struck down as a whole. Option C wrongly places multi-state societies under State legislative power. Option D treats a dissent as the law of the case.
questions.clat_trap: The assumption that a defect in the amending process voids the entire amendment is tempting; the Court's partial striking down is the nuance.
questions.language_trick: 'only' and 'multi-state' limit the situation; read the scope carefully.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: The Court struck down Part IXB in its entirety, including for multi-state societies and Union Territories
options.B: The ratification defect did not touch the addition of 'co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c)
options.C: The 97th Amendment was passed by Parliament with the special majority but without ratification by half of the States
options.D: The Court's reasoning resembles the treatment of paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule in Kihoto Hollohan

questions.explanation: The Court read down the invalidity to State cooperative societies. The statement that the Part was struck down in its entirety contradicts the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D each state something the passage affirms.
questions.clat_trap: A NOT-stem asks for the false statement; three true statements sit beside the false one, and a hurried reader marks the first true-looking option.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT consistent' reverses the usual hunt for the true option.

questions.question: The dissent of K.M. Joseph J. differed from the majority principally in that he

options.A: accepted that Part IXB was invalid for State societies but saw no remedy available
options.B: would have upheld Part IXB in full, treating its effect on State legislative power as incidental to Article 19(1)(c)
options.C: would have struck down Part IXB for multi-state societies as well as for State societies
options.D: held that the 97th Amendment needed ratification by half the States but that the defect could be cured later by Parliament through a fresh enactment

questions.explanation: The dissent saw no constitutional defect that would invalidate Part IXB and upheld it in its entirety.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a cure-by-later-ratification holding. Option C would make the dissent harsher than the majority, which is the reverse of the passage. Option D attributes agreement on invalidity that the dissent did not share.
questions.clat_trap: A dissent is easily confused with the majority's partial position; only an option reflecting complete validity matches the dissent.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: After the decision, Parliament enacts a statute applying Part IXB-style board rules to a cooperative society registered under a State Act and working in only one State. On the passage, such a statute would be

options.A: valid, because the amendment to Article 19(1)(c) authorises central regulation of all cooperative societies in the country
options.B: vulnerable only if it also reserves seats for women or Scheduled Castes on the board of the society
options.C: valid, because Parliament always has residuary power over every cooperative society, wherever it is registered or works
options.D: vulnerable, because the same missing ratification affects any extension of those rules to State-governed societies

questions.explanation: Part IXB's rules were invalid for State societies due to missing ratification; a statute replicating them for a State society faces the same federal objection.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A uses 'always' and misplaces the subject, which sits in the State List. Option B stretches a fundamental-right amendment into a legislative power. Option C narrows the defect to one feature when the problem was legislative competence.
questions.clat_trap: The hypothetical asks you to apply a procedural ruling to a new legislative step; a tempting reading is that the cure lies in the content of the rules.
questions.language_trick: 'Part IXB-style' signals that the same logic, not the same provision, is being tested.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The challenge to Part IXB succeeded even though the changes to Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43B were not challenged on the ground of ratification. Reason (R): The proviso to Article 368(2) is attracted where an amendment affects the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, as Part IXB did with Entry 32 of the State List.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Ratification is triggered by the effect on legislative powers. Part IXB had that effect; the fundamental-right and directive changes did not need ratification on that ground.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Both statements are consistent with the passage, and R supplies the reason why only Part IXB was vulnerable.
questions.clat_trap: Assertion-reason items tempt students to mark 'R is not the explanation' because R reads like a general rule; here the general rule is precisely the cause.
questions.language_trick: 'even though' signals a contrast that R resolves.

passages.title: The 102nd, 104th and 105th Amendments and the Maratha Reservation Case
passages.passage: Reservation for socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs) has been reshaped by three recent amendments. The 102nd Amendment (2018) made the National Commission for Backward Classes a constitutional body under Article 338B and added Article 342A, under which the President, after consulting the Governor, specifies the SEBCs of each State or Union Territory, and Parliament alone may change that list by law. In Dr Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v Chief Minister (May 2021), a five-judge Bench considered the Maharashtra SEBC Act, 2018, which gave a separate quota to the Maratha community and took total reservation beyond the 50 per cent ceiling laid down in Indra Sawhney (1992). The Bench was unanimous in striking down the quota, holding that no 'extraordinary circumstances' justifying a breach of the ceiling had been shown, and it declined to refer Indra Sawhney to a larger Bench. On the effect of the 102nd Amendment, however, it was divided 3:2: the majority held that after the amendment only the President, acting on the Commission's advice, may identify SEBCs for the Central list, and that States may only make recommendations; the minority held that States retained the power to identify SEBCs for their own purposes. Parliament responded with the 105th Amendment (August 2021), which added clause (3) to Article 342A, restoring to States and Union Territories the power to prepare their own lists of SEBCs, while leaving the President's power under clause (1) over the Central list intact. Separately, the 104th Amendment (2019) extended the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies under Article 334 until 25 January 2030, and ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Articles 331 and 333. The 50 per cent ceiling itself remains contested; the EWS quota later upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022) was treated by the majority there as a separate category.

questions.question: The Maratha quota under the Maharashtra SEBC Act, 2018 was struck down because

options.A: Indra Sawhney had been overruled and a fresh ceiling of 40 per cent had been fixed
options.B: the 102nd Amendment had taken away every legislative power of the State over backward classes
options.C: the 50 per cent ceiling stood and no extraordinary circumstances had been shown to cross it
options.D: the Maratha community was held to be a forward community not entitled to any State benefit

questions.explanation: The unanimous holding was that the ceiling remained and the State failed to show extraordinary circumstances.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents an overruling and a new figure. Option B makes a finding about the community that the passage does not record. Option D confuses the 3:2 point on the Central list with the ground of invalidity.
questions.clat_trap: The 3:2 split on the 102nd Amendment is the headline feature, which makes some students think it caused the invalidity; the actual ground was unanimous.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: After the 105th Amendment, State X wishes to list a community as SEBC for the purposes of State reservation. It may

options.A: rely on the minority view in Jaishri Patil, which now binds all High Courts on the powers of the States
options.B: prepare its own list under the newly added clause of Article 342A, without disturbing the Central list
options.C: only recommend the community to the President, who alone can notify it as a backward class for every purpose, State or Central
options.D: notify the community through the Governor, but only after Parliament amends the Central list by an Act of its own

questions.explanation: The 105th Amendment added clause (3) to Article 342A so that States and Union Territories can prepare their own lists; the President's power over the Central list remains.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reflects the position under the 3:2 majority before the amendment. Option C invents a precondition. Option D treats a minority view as binding.
questions.clat_trap: The majority holding in Jaishri Patil is superseded for State lists by the 105th Amendment; students who forget the later amendment mark the earlier position.
questions.language_trick: 'for the purposes of State reservation' limits the question to State lists.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs an amendment with its effect correctly?

options.A: 104th Amendment: inserted clause (3) of Article 342A and restored the State power over SEBC lists
options.B: 104th Amendment: extended SC/ST seat reservation in legislatures to 25 January 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination
options.C: 105th Amendment: made the National Commission for Backward Classes a constitutional body under Article 338B
options.D: 102nd Amendment: allowed States to prepare their own SEBC lists and raised the ceiling to 60 per cent

questions.explanation: Only the 104th Amendment pairing is accurate. The constitutional status of the Commission came with the 102nd and the State list power with the 105th.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A attributes the 105th Amendment's work, and a ceiling change, to the 102nd. Option C gives the 102nd's work to the 105th. Option D gives the 105th's work to the 104th.
questions.clat_trap: Numbers of amendments blur together; the trap rests on a deliberate swap of two or three amendments with plausible effects.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: How did the Jaishri Patil Bench treat Indra Sawhney?

options.A: It declined to reconsider it and kept the ceiling intact, finding no extraordinary circumstances
options.B: It overruled it in part by relaxing the ceiling for communities with a history of agitation and backwardness
options.C: It referred it to a larger Bench but suspended the Maratha quota in the meantime
options.D: It held that the ceiling applies only to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes

questions.explanation: The Bench refused to refer Indra Sawhney to a larger Bench and applied the ceiling.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B imagines a partial overruling. Option C limits the ceiling to a different group. Option D adds a reference that never took place.
questions.clat_trap: After a landmark case is questioned, students assume the Court must have moved it; here it held the line.
questions.language_trick: 'declined to reconsider' is the exact phrase to hold on to.

questions.question: The 3:2 division in Jaishri Patil concerned

options.A: whether Article 15(4) permits any reservation for backward classes in education
options.B: whether, after the 102nd Amendment, States may themselves identify SEBCs for the Central list
options.C: whether Indra Sawhney should be referred to a larger Bench for reconsideration
options.D: whether the Maratha quota crossed the 50 per cent ceiling without any extraordinary circumstances

questions.explanation: The division was only on the effect of the 102nd Amendment. The ceiling, the absence of extraordinary circumstances and the refusal to reconsider Indra Sawhney were unanimous.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option C were unanimous points. Option D was not in issue.
questions.clat_trap: A split decision seems to split on everything; the question tests which issue was divided.
questions.language_trick: 'concerned' with a narrow scope requires isolating one issue.

questions.question: Consider the statements: I. The 102nd Amendment made the National Commission for Backward Classes a constitutional body. II. Jaishri Patil struck down the Maratha quota for breaching the 50 per cent ceiling without extraordinary circumstances. III. The 105th Amendment restored the States' power to prepare SEBC lists. IV. Jaishri Patil overruled Indra Sawhney. Which statements are correct?

options.A: II, III and IV only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: I and IV only
options.D: I, II, III and IV

questions.explanation: Statements I, II and III are in the passage. Statement IV is wrong, since the Bench refused to reconsider Indra Sawhney.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement IV is the only incorrect one, which removes every option that contains it.
questions.clat_trap: The false statement is the one students most associate with a landmark reservation case; the other three are dull facts they may overlook.
questions.language_trick: 'Which statements are correct' means exclude the wrong one.

passages.title: Basic Structure, the Ninth Schedule and Legislative Override
passages.passage: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), a Bench of thirteen judges divided 7:6 and held that Parliament's power under Article 368 extends to amending any provision of the Constitution but does not extend to altering its basic structure. The decision overruled Golak Nath (1967), which had barred amendment of fundamental rights altogether, and upheld the first part of Article 31C. In Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975), clause (4) of Article 329A, inserted by the 39th Amendment to protect the Prime Minister's election, was struck down as it violated free and fair elections and the rule of law. In Minerva Mills (1980), clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 and an expanded Article 31C inserted by the 42nd Amendment were held invalid. The Ninth Schedule, added by the First Amendment through Article 31B, shields listed laws from challenge for violation of fundamental rights. In Waman Rao (1981) the Court held that laws placed in it before 24 April 1973, the date of Kesavananda, remain protected, while later inclusions are open to challenge. In I.R. Coelho (2007), nine judges held that a law included after that date can be tested against fundamental rights that form part of the basic structure, including the combination of Articles 14, 19 and 21. More recently, in Madras Bar Association v Union of India (November 2021), provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 on minimum age of fifty years for tribunal members and short four-year tenures were struck down as undermining the separation of powers and judicial independence. The Court said that the legislature may remove the basis on which a judgment rests by curing the defects, but it cannot simply re-enact the same provisions in order to override the verdict. The doctrine thus continues to guide courts, and Kesavananda's fifty years were marked in 2023.

questions.question: The central holding of Kesavananda Bharati is that

options.A: Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution but may not destroy or alter its basic structure
options.B: fundamental rights can never be amended by Parliament for any purpose whatsoever
options.C: Parliament enjoys unlimited power under Article 368 so long as the special majority is obtained
options.D: courts may review a constitutional amendment only for compliance with its procedure

questions.explanation: Kesavananda replaced the absolute bar of Golak Nath with a limit tied to basic structure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states the overruled Golak Nath view in absolute terms. Option C is the opposite of a limited amending power. Option D limits review to procedure, a position the Bench rejected.
questions.clat_trap: Absolute words ('never', 'unlimited', 'only') mark options as extreme; only the middle path survives.
questions.language_trick: 'any part ... but may not destroy' balances breadth and limit.

questions.question: A law added to the Ninth Schedule in 1985 allegedly violates Article 21 in a way that affects the basic structure. On the passage, the law is

options.A: immune from challenge, because Article 31B protects every law placed in the Schedule from all fundamental rights
options.B: open to challenge on that ground, as post-1973 inclusions can be tested against basic-structure rights
options.C: challengeable only if it also violates the federal structure of the Constitution
options.D: immune, because Waman Rao protects all laws placed in the Schedule before 2007

questions.explanation: Waman Rao draws the line at 24 April 1973 and Coelho allows review of later inclusions against fundamental rights forming the basic structure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the post-1973 review. Option C narrows review to federalism. Option D misstates the cut-off date.
questions.clat_trap: The trap is the date: students see 'Ninth Schedule' and assume complete immunity, or confuse the 1973 line with the 2007 decision.
questions.language_trick: '1985' is the fact that decides which side of the line the law falls on.

questions.question: Following Madras Bar Association, Parliament enacts a new tribunal law repeating the same minimum age and tenure rules in identical words, intending to override the judgment. On the passage, the new law is

options.A: likely invalid, as re-enacting the same defects does not remove the basis of the judgment
options.B: valid, because Parliament may always override a judgment by passing a fresh law
options.C: invalid only if the Court declares each provision unconstitutional afresh in a new proceeding
options.D: valid, because the Court has no power to review a law dealing with tribunals

questions.explanation: The Court allows curing of the defect that formed the basis of the judgment but not a bare override through re-enactment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B uses 'always' and ignores the cure-versus-override distinction. Option C ignores the Court's review power. Option D confuses the need for a new challenge with validity.
questions.clat_trap: The distinction between curing a defect and overriding a verdict is subtle; the hypothetical sets identical wording to test it.
questions.language_trick: 'in identical words' is the language trick: the defect has not been cured.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct on the passage?

options.A: Waman Rao protected Ninth Schedule laws placed before 24 April 1973
options.B: Coelho tested later Ninth Schedule laws against basic-structure rights
options.C: Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain upheld the 39th Amendment's protection of the Prime Minister's election
options.D: Minerva Mills struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, which the 42nd Amendment had inserted into it

questions.explanation: Raj Narain struck down the protective clause, as it violated free and fair elections.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option B and Option D are accurately stated.
questions.clat_trap: A NOT-stem with three accurate decoys: the only wrong one is the reversal of a holding.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT correct' calls for the incorrect option.

questions.question: The phrase 'golden triangle' in the basic-structure discussion refers to the combination of

options.A: Articles 14, 19 and 21
options.B: Articles 14, 15 and 16, read together as the guarantee of equality
options.C: Articles 19, 25 and 26, grouped as the freedoms of expression and conscience
options.D: Articles 21, 22 and 32, taken together as the core of the personal liberty remedies

questions.explanation: Coelho treated the combined operation of Articles 14, 19 and 21 as part of the basic structure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are other clusters of rights that do not form the triangle.
questions.clat_trap: Recall-based item with plausible clusters from Part III; the trap is the familiarity of Articles 15, 16 and 22.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The minimum-age rule for tribunal members was struck down in Madras Bar Association as infringing separation of powers. Reason (R): Parliament can never re-enact a provision once the Supreme Court has struck it down.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A follows from the passage. R is too absolute: the Court allows a cure that removes the basis of the judgment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R fails because of 'never'; the same passage that supports A rebuts R.
questions.clat_trap: Students read R as a general principle of judicial supremacy and accept it; the absolute word is the flaw.
questions.language_trick: 'never' and 'can never' signal overstatement.

passages.title: The 86th Amendment, the Right to Education and Minority Institutions
passages.passage: The 86th Amendment of 2002 inserted Article 21A, which provides free and compulsory education to children between six and fourteen years in such manner as the State may by law determine. It also altered Article 45 so that the Directive Principle now concerns early childhood care for children below six, and added Article 51A(k), a fundamental duty of parents and guardians to provide opportunities for education. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 followed. Before the amendment, the Court in Unni Krishnan (1993) had held that the right to education up to fourteen flows from Article 21. In Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan (2012), a three-judge Bench upheld the Act's requirement that private unaided schools admit twenty-five per cent children from weaker sections, but held that the requirement does not apply to minority schools. In Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v Union of India (May 2014), a five-judge Bench held that applying Article 21A and the Act to aided or unaided minority institutions would abrogate the right under Article 30(1), so the Act cannot bind them. In the same decision, Article 15(5), inserted by the 93rd Amendment (2005) to permit reservation in private unaided institutions other than minority institutions, was upheld. Earlier, in Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008), the 93rd Amendment and twenty-seven per cent OBC reservation in central educational institutions were upheld with exclusion of the creamy layer. The broader backdrop is T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002), where eleven judges held that private institutions can be established under Article 19(1)(g) and minority status is determined State-wise, with capitation fees barred.

questions.question: Article 21A, as inserted by the 86th Amendment, guarantees

options.A: early childhood care for children below six as an enforceable fundamental right
options.B: free education in State schools only, without any compulsory element
options.C: free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen, as the State may determine by law
options.D: free education to every person up to the age of eighteen as a self-executing and directly enforceable right

questions.explanation: Article 21A covers ages six to fourteen and leaves the manner to State law. Early childhood care went to Article 45.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A misstates age and enforceability. Option B confuses Article 21A with the Directive Principle in Article 45. Option D drops the word 'compulsory'.
questions.clat_trap: Numbers and categories are easy to blur; the options borrow features of Article 45 and Article 51A(k).
questions.language_trick: 'in such manner as the State may by law determine' is a classic phrase.

questions.question: Which category of school is bound by the 25 per cent admission requirement under the Act, after the 2012 and 2014 decisions?

options.A: Only minority schools that receive aid from the State
options.B: All private schools, including minority institutions, whether aided or unaided
options.C: Only government and local authority schools
options.D: Private unaided schools that are not minority institutions

questions.explanation: Society for Unaided Private Schools upheld the quota for unaided non-minority schools; Pramati excluded minority institutions, whether aided or not.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the minority exemption. Option B reverses the position. Option C narrows the quota to a class that already provides free education.
questions.clat_trap: Combining two decisions: the 2012 case dealt with unaided schools, the 2014 case extended the exemption to aided minority schools.
questions.language_trick: 'after the 2012 and 2014 decisions' requires reading both.

questions.question: In Pramati, the Court held the Act inapplicable to minority institutions because

options.A: T.M.A. Pai had already held that minority schools are wholly excluded from every statute on education, including those on admission and fees
options.B: its application would abrogate the minorities' right to establish and administer institutions under Article 30(1)
options.C: Article 15(5) bars the State from legislating for any private educational institution
options.D: Article 21A binds only State-run schools and cannot reach any private institution

questions.explanation: The reasoning is based on Article 30(1): obligations such as admitting twenty-five per cent from outside the community would abrogate it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the 2012 holding for unaided non-minority schools. Option C reverses Article 15(5), which enables reservation in private unaided institutions. Option D overstates T.M.A. Pai, which did not exempt minority schools from all regulation.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options borrow real cases and provisions; only one uses the correct constitutional hook.
questions.language_trick: 'abrogate' signals a total destruction of the right and not mere regulation.

questions.question: Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) is correctly described as upholding

options.A: the 93rd Amendment only so far as it concerns Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
options.B: the 93rd Amendment and 27 per cent OBC reservation in central institutions, with the creamy layer excluded
options.C: the 86th Amendment and compulsory admission of twenty-five per cent weaker-section children in private unaided schools
options.D: Article 15(5) for minority institutions and State-wise determination of minority status

questions.explanation: The decision dealt with OBC reservation in central educational institutions and excluded the creamy layer.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A mixes the 2012 and 2014 education cases. Option C limits the holding to the wrong groups. Option D mixes Pramati and T.M.A. Pai.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option gathers pieces from other cases in the passage, so recall of the match between case and issue is tested.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A State-aided minority school refuses to admit twenty-five per cent children from weaker sections, citing Pramati. On the passage, the refusal is

options.A: unsustainable, since the school receives State aid and Article 21A binds every aided institution in the same way as a government school
options.B: unsustainable, since Article 15(5) was upheld in the very same decision
options.C: sustainable, as the Act's obligations cannot be applied to minority institutions, aided or unaided
options.D: sustainable only if the school is unaided, since aid brings the school within the reach of Article 21A

questions.explanation: Pramati covers aided and unaided minority institutions alike.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the extension to aided minority schools. Option B limits the protection to unaided schools. Option D misreads Article 15(5), which itself excludes minority institutions.
questions.clat_trap: Aid is the red herring: students link aid to State control and mark unsustainable.
questions.language_trick: 'aided or unaided' is the phrase that removes the aid distinction.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The 86th Amendment converted the right to education, already recognised judicially for children up to fourteen, into an express fundamental right. Reason (R): Unni Krishnan (1993) had held that the right to education up to fourteen flows from Article 21.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are in the passage. R records the prior judicial recognition, which is the background of A but not the cause of the amendment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R describes a judgment that preceded the amendment; it does not explain why Parliament chose to insert Article 21A.
questions.clat_trap: Students treat any true background fact as the explanation; the reason must explain the assertion and not merely precede it.
questions.language_trick: 'already recognised' signals that R is background and not cause.

passages.title: The 44th Amendment, Property, Emergency and Article 300A
passages.passage: The 44th Amendment of 1978 reshaped the Constitution after the Emergency. It removed the right to property from Part III by omitting Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, and inserted Article 300A: no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law. Articles 31A, 31B and 31C continued. It also replaced 'internal disturbance' in Article 352 by 'armed rebellion', required written advice of the Cabinet to the President for proclaiming an Emergency, and amended Article 359 to provide that the enforcement of rights under Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended during an Emergency. The background was ADM Jabalpur (1976), in which the majority held that Article 21 could not be enforced while the Emergency lasted; the decision was later disapproved in Puttaswamy (2017). In K.T. Plantation (2011), the Court held that Article 300A requires a valid law and a public purpose, but that compensation is not automatically required in every case. In Vidya Devi v State of Himachal Pradesh (2020), the Court described the right to property as a constitutional and human right, and held that the State, having taken the appellant's land without any authority of law decades earlier, could not plead adverse possession against her. In Kolkata Municipal Corporation v Bimal Kumar Shah (May 2024), a seven-judge Bench held that Article 300A carries seven procedural entitlements for the owner: notice, hearing, a reasoned decision, a public purpose, compensation, an efficient and expeditious process, and conclusion of the proceedings. The Bench noted that the right is no longer fundamental, but that the State's power to deprive remains subject to these safeguards.

questions.question: After the 44th Amendment, the right to property is best described as

options.A: a Directive Principle that courts cannot enforce in any proceeding
options.B: a constitutional right under Article 300A, no longer a fundamental right in Part III
options.C: a statutory right that exists only where Parliament has enacted a protective law
options.D: a fundamental right in Part III, with compensation fixed at the market value of the property

questions.explanation: The amendment omitted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and placed the right in Article 300A.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A wrongly keeps it in Part III. Option C demotes it to a non-enforceable principle. Option D treats it as an ordinary statutory right rather than a constitutional one.
questions.clat_trap: Students sometimes assume the right vanished entirely or remained a fundamental right; the intermediate category is the answer.
questions.language_trick: 'no longer a fundamental right' limits the loss.

questions.question: The State seized a family's land in 1967 without any law, and still holds it. In 2024 the State claims title by adverse possession. Under Vidya Devi, the claim

options.A: fails, as the State cannot plead adverse possession for a dispossession carried out without authority of law
options.B: succeeds, since decades of uninterrupted possession ripen into title against any private owner, whoever the possessor may be
options.C: fails only if the family proves that no compensation was ever paid to them for the land
options.D: succeeds, since Article 300A protects the State's possession of land as much as it protects the property of a private person

questions.explanation: Vidya Devi held the State cannot rely on adverse possession where it took land without authority of law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores that the dispossession was unlawful. Option C misuses Article 300A. Option D makes compensation the test when the lack of legal authority is the ground.
questions.clat_trap: Adverse possession is typically used against private owners; the question tests whether this extends to a State acting without law.
questions.language_trick: 'without any law' is the fact that decides.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the procedural entitlements of an owner under Article 300A as described in Bimal Kumar Shah?

options.A: A right to veto the acquisition if the owner objects to the public purpose
options.B: A right to notice and to be heard before deprivation of the property takes place, as a first step of the process
options.C: A right to a reasoned decision on the objections and to compensation for the property taken from the owner
options.D: A right to an efficient and expeditious process that concludes within a reasonable time, without needless delay

questions.explanation: The seven entitlements include notice, hearing, a reasoned decision, public purpose, compensation, efficiency and conclusion. They do not include a veto.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are among the seven entitlements.
questions.clat_trap: The false option sounds protective and plausible; students prefer rights over restrictions.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT' reverses the search; 'veto' is the invented right.

questions.question: Article 359, as amended by the 44th Amendment, means that during an Emergency

options.A: only the right under Article 21 is protected, while Article 20 may be suspended
options.B: Articles 14 and 19 are protected, while Articles 20 and 21 may be suspended
options.C: the enforcement of every right in Part III may be suspended by Presidential order
options.D: the enforcement of rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended

questions.explanation: The amendment immunised Articles 20 and 21 against suspension.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the pre-amendment position in general terms. Option B halves the protection. Option C reverses the protected articles.
questions.clat_trap: The pre-amendment and post-amendment positions are mixed in the options; a student who remembers ADM Jabalpur only marks the first.
questions.language_trick: 'cannot be suspended' is a strong phrase from the passage.

questions.question: On K.T. Plantation, which statement about Article 300A is correct?

options.A: Compensation at full market value is a condition of every deprivation of property under the Article
options.B: A law is needed, but a public purpose is not, since the Article is silent on it
options.C: A valid law and public purpose are needed, but compensation is not automatically required
options.D: An executive order suffices, as the Article demands no law

questions.explanation: The Court read in the requirements of a law and a public purpose but not an automatic compensation requirement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A keeps the old Article 31 position. Option B drops the requirement of law. Option D drops the public purpose requirement.
questions.clat_trap: Distractors preserve the pre-44th compensation rule or drop a requirement that the Court read into Article 300A.
questions.language_trick: 'not automatically required' limits the answer.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The 44th Amendment overruled ADM Jabalpur. Reason (R): The 44th Amendment provided that enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during an Emergency.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R is correct. A is incorrect because the amendment changed Article 359 but did not overrule the decision, which was disapproved later in Puttaswamy.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A attributes to the amendment what the Court did decades later.
questions.clat_trap: The amendment responded to ADM Jabalpur, so students equate response with overruling; only a court can overrule a judgment.
questions.language_trick: 'overruled' is a term for courts, not constitutional amendments.

passages.title: Article 356, the Forty-fourth Amendment and Bommai: Emergency Powers over the States
passages.passage: Article 356 allows the President, on a Governor's report or otherwise, to proclaim that the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. Under the Forty-fourth Amendment a proclamation must be approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament within two months, failing which it ceases to operate. An approved proclamation lasts six months and may be extended in six-month steps; it cannot run beyond one year unless a proclamation of national emergency is in operation and the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held, and in no case beyond three years. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a nine-judge Bench held that a proclamation is justiciable, that the Court may test whether relevant material exists, and that the Assembly cannot be dissolved before Parliament approves the proclamation; until then it may only be suspended. If the proclamation is found invalid, the Court may restore the dismissed government and the Assembly. The Bench treated secularism and federalism as part of the basic structure and said that the floor of the House, not the Governor's subjective assessment, is the place to test a ministry's majority. Rameshwar Prasad (2006) held the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly to be mala fide. Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) had earlier taken a narrower view of judicial review. President's rule was imposed in Manipur on 13 February 2025; its later course should be verified from current sources. Article 355 casts a duty on the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure that its government is carried on in accordance with the Constitution, while Article 365 treats a State's failure to comply with Union directions as a circumstance in which the constitutional machinery may be taken to have failed.

questions.question: A proclamation under Article 356 is approved by the Lok Sabha within two months, but the Rajya Sabha does not take it up before the two months end. The position is that the proclamation

options.A: ceases to operate at the end of two months, because resolutions of both Houses are needed for approval
options.B: continues for six months, since the Lok Sabha, as the House of the People, is the only House whose approval is decisive
options.C: continues until the Election Commission certifies that fresh elections to the State can be held
options.D: remains in force until the Rajya Sabha next meets, which may decide the matter in its following session

questions.explanation: Approval needs resolutions of both Houses within two months. Absence of approval by one House means the proclamation lapses.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B gives the Lok Sabha a primacy that the Article does not provide. Option C invents an open-ended wait for the Rajya Sabha. Option D misuses the Election Commission certificate, which relates only to extension beyond one year.
questions.clat_trap: The Lok Sabha-primacy intuition from money bills and the no-confidence motion tempts students to prefer it.
questions.language_trick: 'both Houses' and 'within two months' fix the test.

questions.question: On the same day that a proclamation is issued, the Union dissolves the State Assembly without waiting for Parliament. On the passage, the dissolution

options.A: is valid if the Governor's report states that the ministry had lost its majority in the House
options.B: is open to being held invalid, because until Parliament approves, the Assembly may only be kept in suspended animation
options.C: stands valid, because the President takes over legislative powers of the State under the proclamation itself
options.D: is beyond judicial scrutiny, because the satisfaction on which the proclamation rests is purely political

questions.explanation: Bommai held that dissolution before parliamentary approval is impermissible; the Assembly can only be suspended in the meantime.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses the power to take over functions with the power to dissolve. Option C contradicts the holding that proclamations are justiciable. Option D treats the Governor's view as conclusive, which the Bench rejected.
questions.clat_trap: A statement that the ministry lost its majority sounds like a good reason for dissolution, but the sequence of events is what the Court tested.
questions.language_trick: 'until then' marks a temporary state of suspension.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the position in Bommai as described in the passage?

options.A: A proclamation may be tested by the Court for the existence of relevant material
options.B: The Court may restore a dismissed government if the proclamation is found invalid
options.C: The Governor's assessment that a ministry has lost its majority is conclusive, so a floor test is unnecessary
options.D: Secularism and federalism have been treated as part of the basic structure

questions.explanation: The Bench said the floor of the House is the proper place to test a majority, not the Governor's subjective assessment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is part of the holding on justiciability. Option B is stated in the passage. Option D is stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A 'NOT' stem makes the three consistent statements decoys, and the wrong statement is a plausible one.
questions.language_trick: 'conclusive' is the absolute word that signals the incorrect proposition.

questions.question: A proclamation under Article 356 was approved on 1 January 2026 and extended twice in six-month steps. At the end of one year no national emergency is in operation. The proclamation

options.A: may be extended for six months more, if the Election Commission certifies that holding elections is difficult
options.B: may be extended without limit, if the President is satisfied that the State government cannot be carried on
options.C: cannot be extended again, since one year is the outer limit unless the national emergency condition is also met
options.D: may be extended up to three years by a resolution of Parliament alone, since three years is the stated outer ceiling in the Article

questions.explanation: Beyond one year both conditions must exist: a proclamation of national emergency and an Election Commission certificate. Without national emergency, one year is the limit.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the one-year bar. Option B counts only one condition. Option D drops the three-year ceiling altogether.
questions.clat_trap: The Election Commission certificate alone seems enough, but the passage requires it along with a national emergency.
questions.language_trick: 'unless' and 'in no case' set the layered limits.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) held that the Court has no power at all to examine a proclamation under Article 356. Reason (R): Bommai (1994) later held that a proclamation is justiciable to the extent of testing whether relevant material exists.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The 1977 decision took only a narrower view of review; it did not bar review altogether. The later holding on justiciability is correctly stated.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is correctly reported from the passage. A overstates the older case, which was narrower but not an absolute bar.
questions.clat_trap: A and R look like a before-and-after pair, so the pair seems to explain A; the catch is that A exaggerates the earlier decision.
questions.language_trick: 'no power at all' is the overstated phrase; the passage says 'narrower view'.

questions.question: Which statement about Articles 355 and 365 is accurate on the passage?

options.A: Article 365 applies only to Union Territories, where there is no Governor to report on the failure of the machinery
options.B: Article 365 treats a State's failure to follow Union directions as a sign that constitutional machinery has failed
options.C: Article 355 imposes on each State the duty to protect the Union against external aggression and internal disturbance
options.D: Article 355 itself authorises the President to dismiss a State ministry whenever internal disturbance occurs anywhere in the State concerned

questions.explanation: Article 365 supplies a ground for proclamation; Article 355 is a duty on the Union, not a power to dismiss.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns a duty into a power. Option C invents a limit to Union Territories. Option D reverses the direction of the duty.
questions.clat_trap: Students who know Article 355 only as the 'duty' clause reverse its subject and object.
questions.language_trick: 'casts a duty on the Union' tells who the duty-bearer is.

passages.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: New Offences and Old Debates
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, in force from 1 July 2024, replaces the Indian Penal Code, 1860, reorganising offences and adding new ones. Organised crime is defined in section 111 as continuing unlawful activity such as kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offences or cyber-crime, committed by a member of an organised crime syndicate, singly or jointly, by violence, threat, intimidation, coercion or other unlawful means to gain material benefit. Section 112 deals separately with petty organised crime, such as theft by gangs, snatching, cheating and unauthorised sale of tickets. Section 113 defines a terrorist act by the intent to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty or security of India or to strike terror in the people. Murder by a group of five or more persons acting in concert on the ground of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any similar ground is punishable under section 103(2) with death or imprisonment for life, and fine. Section 152 punishes acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, committed by words, signs, visible representation, electronic communication or financial means, and takes the place of the offence of sedition in section 124A of the IPC; in 2022 the Supreme Court in S. G. Vombatkere kept section 124A in abeyance, and the status of challenges to section 152 should be verified. Section 69 punishes sexual intercourse by deceitful means, which expressly includes a false promise of marriage, where the act does not amount to rape. The Sanhita adds community service as a form of punishment for certain petty offences. Adultery, struck down in Joseph Shine (2018), and the offence in section 377 of the IPC are not retained.

questions.question: Five men beat a man to death because of his caste. On the passage, each of the five is liable

options.A: under the provision on organised crime, because five persons acting together in concert form an organised syndicate
options.B: only if shown to have struck the very blow that caused death, since criminal liability is individual in such cases
options.C: for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, since no common intention to kill is evident
options.D: under the provision on group murder, punishable with death or life imprisonment, and fine

questions.explanation: The provision on murder by a group of five or more on listed grounds, including caste, applies and punishes each participant.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the group-murder provision. Option B lowers the offence without basis. Option C mixes the new provisions: organised crime needs continuing unlawful activity for material benefit, not a single act driven by caste.
questions.clat_trap: Because organised crime is the 'group' offence best known to students, the more specific provision is overlooked.
questions.language_trick: 'acting in concert' signals group liability.

questions.question: Three persons, as members of a syndicate, regularly snatch mobile phones from commuters in a city to make money. Their conduct falls most directly under

options.A: petty organised crime, as snatching is among the offences that provision lists
options.B: ordinary theft alone, since the new group provisions require use of lethal violence
options.C: the provision on terrorist acts, since commuters are put in fear
options.D: organised crime, since a syndicate, continuing unlawful activity and material gain are all present on these facts

questions.explanation: Snatching committed by a gang is specifically listed as petty organised crime, which controls over the general category.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B overlooks the specific list for petty offences. Option C ignores that the specific provision governs. Option D adds a requirement that the passage does not contain.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'syndicate' tempts the choice of the more serious provision, although the nature of the offence decides the category.
questions.language_trick: 'regularly' and 'snatch' point to the petty category.

questions.question: The passage states that the Supreme Court in 2022 'kept section 124A in abeyance'. Which inference is best supported?

options.A: Section 152 is valid, because the Court upheld sedition in 2022 and merely paused its use pending a fuller review
options.B: The 2022 order concerned the IPC offence and does not by itself suspend section 152
options.C: Section 152 is void, because the Court has struck down the offence of sedition in all its forms
options.D: Section 152 is confined to spoken or written words, as was the offence it replaces

questions.explanation: The order paused the IPC provision. It neither struck down sedition nor addressed the new section, and its challenge status remains to be verified.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A equates abeyance with striking down. Option C equates abeyance with upholding. Option D contradicts the passage, which lists several modes of commission.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'abeyance' is neither a strike-down nor an upholding; a student who reads it as either goes wrong.
questions.language_trick: 'in abeyance' means suspended, not decided.

questions.question: A man, without any intention of marrying, promises marriage to a woman and has consensual intercourse with her. The act does not amount to rape. The man is

options.A: liable for rape, since consent obtained by a false promise is no consent in law
options.B: liable only if the promise of marriage was made in writing and signed by the man
options.C: not liable, since the woman consented to the act and consent is a complete answer to every sexual offence
options.D: liable under the provision on deceitful sexual intercourse, which includes a false promise of marriage

questions.explanation: The provision on deceitful means expressly includes a false promise of marriage where the act is not rape.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the express inclusion. Option B converts a lesser offence into rape in contradiction with the stem. Option C adds a formal requirement not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The stem says the act is not rape, closing off the aggravated option while keeping 'consent' alive as a decoy.
questions.language_trick: 'does not amount to rape' defines the residual scope of the section.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Section 69 can apply to a man who induces consensual intercourse by a false promise of marriage. Reason (R): Section 69 applies only where the act does not amount to rape.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is true, as the section expressly covers false promises of marriage. R is also true, but it states a limit on the section's scope, not the reason why consensual intercourse induced by deceit is covered.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is a limiting condition and not the ground on which A rests; the ground is the express mention of deceit and false promise of marriage.
questions.clat_trap: R sounds like a clarification of A, which tempts the choice of the first option.
questions.language_trick: The words 'only where' in R restrict the section; they do not explain A.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: The Sanhita adds community service as a form of punishment for certain petty offences
options.B: Petty organised crime is treated separately from organised crime
options.C: Adultery is not retained as an offence after Joseph Shine
options.D: Section 113 is attracted only when a person has actually died in the attack

questions.explanation: Section 113 depends on intent to threaten unity, integrity, sovereignty or security, or to strike terror; actual death is not required.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is supported by the two separate sections. Option B is stated in the passage. Option C is stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A 'NOT' stem with correct-sounding options means the reader must spot the invented condition.
questions.language_trick: 'only when' adds a requirement of death that the definition does not contain.

passages.title: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023: Procedure Reworked
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), in force from 1 July 2024, replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. It formalises the zero FIR: an FIR may be registered at any police station irrespective of territorial jurisdiction and transferred later to the station that has jurisdiction. Information given electronically must be signed by the informant within three days before the police take it on record. For cognizable offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven, the officer in charge may, with the permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent, hold a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists. The Sanhita allows trial in the absence of a proclaimed offender once charges have been framed and ninety days have passed since the framing, subject to safeguards such as notice and the appointment of a State-funded lawyer. Police custody of up to fifteen days, which under the old Code had to be sought within the first fifteen days of detention, may now be authorised in parts during the first forty or sixty days of the sixty- or ninety-day detention period, depending on the offence. For offences punishable with seven years or more, a forensic expert must visit the crime scene to collect evidence, and search and seizure must be videographed. A judgment is to be pronounced within forty-five days of the conclusion of arguments. Proceedings pending under the Code on the date of commencement continue under it; the BNSS applies to proceedings commenced on or after 1 July 2024, though the exact scope of the savings clause should be verified.

questions.question: A woman reports an offence committed in Pune at a police station in Delhi. The Delhi station

options.A: must register a zero FIR and later transfer it to the station that has jurisdiction
options.B: must obtain a Magistrate's permission before registering an FIR for an offence outside its area
options.C: may refuse, because the offence occurred outside its territorial limits
options.D: registers the FIR and keeps the investigation, since jurisdiction follows the place of registration

questions.explanation: Zero FIR allows registration anywhere; transfer follows.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B describes the older practice that the BNSS departs from. Option C adds a Magistrate's permission not found in the passage. Option D loses the transfer.
questions.clat_trap: Students used to territorial refusals choose the old rule.
questions.language_trick: 'irrespective of territorial jurisdiction' removes the ground for refusal.

questions.question: Information about a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of seven years is given at a police station. On the passage, the officer in charge

options.A: must hold a preliminary enquiry, since offences of seven years or more are the very ones for which it is made compulsory
options.B: may hold a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days with the Deputy Superintendent's permission
options.C: may hold a preliminary enquiry for thirty days with the Magistrate's permission
options.D: has no occasion for a preliminary enquiry, since the permitted band ends below seven years

questions.explanation: The enquiry band is three years or more but less than seven. An offence punishable with seven years falls outside it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A assumes seven is inside the band. Option B invents a thirty-day period and the wrong authority. Option C makes the enquiry mandatory, which the provision does not do.
questions.clat_trap: 'Three to seven years' is casually read as including seven; the passage says 'less than seven'.
questions.language_trick: 'less than seven' excludes seven.

questions.question: Charges against a proclaimed offender are framed on 1 March. The earliest date on which trial in his absence may begin, subject to safeguards, is

options.A: after ninety days from the framing of charges
options.B: after ninety days from the date of the proclamation
options.C: after charges are framed, provided his counsel consents to the trial
options.D: immediately, once he has been declared a proclaimed offender

questions.explanation: The ninety-day period runs from framing of charges.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the waiting period. Option C starts the clock at the wrong event. Option D invents a consent requirement.
questions.clat_trap: Two dates are in play: proclamation and framing of charges; the clock runs from the latter.
questions.language_trick: 'since the framing' fixes the starting point.

questions.question: Which statement about police custody under the BNSS is accurate on the passage?

options.A: The fifteen days may be authorised in parts during the first forty or sixty days of detention
options.B: The fifteen days must be taken continuously in the first fifteen days of detention
options.C: Police custody may extend up to forty or sixty days in total
options.D: Police custody may be sought only after the sixty- or ninety-day detention period has ended

questions.explanation: The total police custody remains fifteen days, but it may be split across a longer window.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states the old Code's rule. Option C stretches the total quantum. Option D reverses the timing.
questions.clat_trap: The numbers fifteen, forty and sixty are easy to interchange.
questions.language_trick: 'up to fifteen days' is the quantum; 'forty or sixty' is the window.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?

options.A: Judgment is to be pronounced within forty-five days of the conclusion of arguments
options.B: A forensic expert must visit where the offence is punishable with seven years or more
options.C: Search and seizure must be videographed
options.D: A forensic expert must visit the scene in every cognizable offence

questions.explanation: The forensic visit is mandated only for offences punishable with seven years or more.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is stated as a duty. Option B is the stated threshold. Option C is stated.
questions.clat_trap: The overstatement 'every' replaces the threshold.
questions.language_trick: 'every cognizable offence' is the overstated option.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A proceeding pending under the Code of Criminal Procedure on 1 July 2024 continues under that Code. Reason (R): The BNSS applies to proceedings commenced before 1 July 2024.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The passage says pending proceedings continue under the Code and that the BNSS applies to proceedings commenced on or after the date. R is false.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A is correct. R is the reverse of the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A and R both talk of 'proceedings' and the date, which hides that R reverses the rule.
questions.language_trick: 'before' versus 'on or after' flips R.

passages.title: Specific Relief Act, 1963 after the 2018 Amendment
passages.passage: Before the 2018 amendment, specific performance of a contract was a discretionary remedy. The amended Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes it the general rule that the court shall enforce the contract, subject to exceptions listed in the statute, such as contracts where compensation in money is adequate relief, contracts based on the personal qualifications of the parties, and contracts that are in their nature determinable. A plaintiff must aver and prove that he has performed, or has always been ready and willing to perform, the essential terms that remain to be performed; readiness is judged on conduct throughout, not only at the date of the suit. The amendment introduces substituted performance: where a party fails to perform, the other, after serving a notice of thirty days, may have the contract performed by a third party or through his own agency at the cost of the defaulting party and recover the expenses; having chosen this route he cannot sue for specific performance of that contract, though he may claim compensation. Courts are restricted from granting injunctions in suits involving infrastructure projects where this would impede or delay them, and special courts are to try such cases. A suit for summary recovery of possession must be brought within six months of dispossession and no appeal or review lies against the decree, though a regular suit on title may follow. The limitation period for a suit for specific performance is three years from the date fixed for performance or, where no date is fixed, from the date the plaintiff has notice of refusal.

questions.question: After the 2018 amendment, a plaintiff proves a breach of an enforceable contract and his readiness and willingness. The court

options.A: retains a general equitable discretion to decline, even where no exception applies
options.B: may grant specific performance only after the plaintiff has attempted substituted performance
options.C: is expected to grant specific performance unless a statutory exception applies
