options.D: must first award damages and grant specific performance only if damages prove inadequate later

questions.explanation: The amendment converts the remedy into a general rule subject to listed exceptions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A describes the pre-amendment position. Option B reverses the sequence. Option D makes substituted performance a pre-condition, which it is not.
questions.clat_trap: The old 'discretion' idea remains in the student's mind.
questions.language_trick: 'general rule' and 'shall enforce' mark the shift.

questions.question: After a thirty-day notice, B has a third party complete the work at a cost of five lakh rupees at the defaulting seller's expense, and then sues S for specific performance of the same contract. The suit

options.A: fails entirely, since the election of substituted performance bars every other relief, including compensation for the breach
options.B: succeeds, since B has recovered only the cost of the work from the seller and has not obtained the performance itself
options.C: succeeds only if the third party's performance turns out to be defective or incomplete
options.D: fails for specific performance, though B may claim compensation and recover the expenses

questions.explanation: Election of substituted performance bars suit for specific performance of that contract, but compensation remains available.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the bar. Option B adds a condition not in the passage. Option C overstates the bar to cover compensation.
questions.clat_trap: Between two extremes ('succeeds' and 'bars every relief') the middle result is correct.
questions.language_trick: 'though he may claim compensation' preserves some relief.

questions.question: In which situation is specific performance most likely to be refused?

options.A: An agreement to convey land where the seller defaults after taking the advance
options.B: A contract to complete a road project, where an injunction is sought to stop the completion
options.C: A contract for the services of a named artist, based on personal skill
options.D: An agreement to sell a flat at an agreed price, where the seller has changed his mind

questions.explanation: Contracts based on the personal qualifications of the parties fall within the statutory exceptions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is an ordinary enforceable sale. Option B concerns an injunction restriction, which supports completion. Option D is a classic case for enforcement.
questions.clat_trap: A decoy: an infrastructure contract does not bar enforcement; the restriction applies to injunctions.
questions.language_trick: 'personal skill' links to the exception.

questions.question: A is dispossessed of his house without consent on 1 January. He sues on 20 July for summary recovery of possession. The suit

options.A: is maintainable, since the period for such suits is three years
options.B: is barred by time, though he may still bring a regular suit on title
options.C: is maintainable, and the decree is appealable like any other decree of a civil court
options.D: is maintainable only if he first proves title

questions.explanation: Six months had passed. The summary remedy is time-barred but a title suit remains.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies the three-year period meant for specific performance. Option C requires title, which the summary remedy does not. Option D ignores the bar on appeal.
questions.clat_trap: Two limitation periods in the passage (three years, six months) are interchanged.
questions.language_trick: 'within six months' governs the summary remedy.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT correct on the passage?

options.A: Courts are restricted from granting injunctions that delay infrastructure projects
options.B: A plaintiff may be refused relief where compensation in money is adequate
options.C: An appeal lies against a decree in a summary suit for recovery of possession
options.D: Special courts are to try suits involving infrastructure projects

questions.explanation: No appeal or review lies against the decree in a summary possession suit.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is correct. Option B is correct. Option D is correct.
questions.clat_trap: A long list with only one false statement.
questions.language_trick: 'no appeal or review lies' is turned around.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A plaintiff seeking specific performance must show continuous readiness and willingness to perform. Reason (R): Readiness is judged on conduct throughout and not only at the date of the suit.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R explains why A is so: the test is continuous because conduct throughout matters.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is the very reason for the continuity requirement in A.
questions.clat_trap: The pair is straightforward but sits among harder items, tempting over-reading.
questions.language_trick: 'continuous' and 'throughout' match.

passages.title: Maintenance and Succession: Shah Bano to Samad, Vineeta Sharma to Arunachala Gounder
passages.passage: In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman who cannot maintain herself may claim maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a secular provision. Parliament responded with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, making the former husband liable to pay mahr and to make a reasonable and fair provision within the iddat period. In Danial Latifi (2001), the Court upheld the Act, reading the liability for reasonable and fair provision as one that is made within the iddat period but may cover the woman's future needs. In Mohd. Abdul Samad v. State of Telangana (July 2024), the Court held that a divorced Muslim woman may petition under section 125 of the Code (now section 144 of the BNSS) and that the 1986 Act is an additional remedy and not a substitute. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), a three-judge Bench held that daughters are coparceners by birth under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 and that the father need not have been alive on 9 September 2005. In Arunachala Gounder (2022), the Court held that the self-acquired property of a Hindu male who died intestate before 1956 devolves by inheritance on his daughter and not by survivorship on his collaterals. In Rajnesh v. Neha (2020), the Court issued guidelines on maintenance, including a disclosure affidavit by both parties.

questions.question: The passage describes the relationship between Shah Bano and the 1986 Act in which way?

options.A: Shah Bano was overruled by the Act, so section 125 of the Code ceased to apply to Muslim women altogether from its commencement
options.B: The Act applied only to marriages after 1986 and left earlier divorcees to the Code
options.C: The Act was struck down in Danial Latifi as it conflicted with the secular remedy
options.D: Parliament legislated after Shah Bano, and Danial Latifi later read the Act to cover the woman's future needs

questions.explanation: The Act was a response; the Court upheld it by a purposive reading.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses Danial Latifi's outcome. Option B mistakes a statute for the overruling of a decision, and the 2024 holding disproves it. Option C invents a prospective limitation.
questions.clat_trap: The legislative response suggests that the Court's view was overruled; the passage shows the reverse.
questions.language_trick: 'upheld' versus 'struck down'.

questions.question: A divorced Muslim woman petitions under section 144 of the BNSS for maintenance. The husband objects that the 1986 Act is exclusive. On the passage, the objection

options.A: fails, as the 1986 Act is an additional remedy and not a substitute for it
options.B: fails only if she has not claimed mahr under the 1986 Act
options.C: succeeds in part, limiting maintenance to the iddat period
options.D: succeeds, since a special enactment overrides a general provision on the same subject matter

questions.explanation: Samad treats the 1986 Act as additional to the secular remedy.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B applies a special-over-general maxim contrary to the holding. Option C partly accepts the exclusivity argument. Option D invents an election requirement.
questions.clat_trap: The special-general maxim tempts students who forget the 2024 case.
questions.language_trick: 'additional remedy' is the key phrase.

questions.question: Which statement is correct on Vineeta Sharma, as described in the passage?

options.A: A daughter's coparcenary status arises by birth and does not depend on the father being alive on the amendment date
options.B: A daughter becomes a coparcener only if her father was alive on 9 September 2005, when the amendment came into force
options.C: A daughter becomes a coparcener only on the death of her father, when succession actually opens to the family property
options.D: A daughter becomes a coparcener only if she was born after the commencement of the amendment in 2005

questions.explanation: Birth confers coparcenary status; the father's survival is not needed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is the view that the Court rejected. Option C defers the status. Option D invents a cut-off.
questions.clat_trap: A date in the passage encourages date-based answers.
questions.language_trick: 'by birth' versus 'father alive'.

questions.question: A Hindu male died intestate in 1953 leaving self-acquired property, a daughter and a brother's son. On the passage, the property goes to

options.A: the State by escheat, as the Succession Act of 1956 had not commenced
options.B: the brother's son, by survivorship
options.C: the daughter and the brother's son in equal shares
options.D: the daughter, by inheritance

questions.explanation: Arunachala Gounder holds that the daughter inherits where the male died intestate before 1956.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies survivorship wrongly. Option B invents equal shares. Option C assumes a gap in the law.
questions.clat_trap: The date before 1956 suggests that no statute applies.
questions.language_trick: 'by inheritance' versus 'survivorship'.

questions.question: According to Rajnesh v. Neha, as described, the maintenance guidelines require

options.A: a disclosure affidavit by both parties
options.B: maintenance fixed at a set percentage of the payer's income
options.C: an affidavit only by the party claiming maintenance
options.D: maintenance only from the date of the final decree

questions.explanation: The guideline requires disclosure by both.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B halves the requirement. Option C and Option D are not in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Options not in the passage may seem plausible from general knowledge.
questions.language_trick: 'both parties' is the key phrase.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Arunachala Gounder depended on the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 for the daughter's share. Reason (R): The male in that case died before 1956.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court relied on the older law, not the 1956 Act, because the death preceded it. A is false and R is true.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states a true fact; it contradicts A rather than explaining it.
questions.clat_trap: Both statements share the year 1956, which suggests a link.
questions.language_trick: 'depended on' is the false claim.

passages.title: Fairness, Reasonableness and Proportionality in Administrative Action
passages.passage: Administrative action in India is tested on three broad footings: legality, procedural fairness and reasonableness. After Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978), Articles 14, 19 and 21 are read together, so that a procedure which deprives a person of life or personal liberty must itself be fair, just and reasonable, and the rules of natural justice are read into statutory silence unless excluded by clear words. Traditionally, review of discretionary power for unreasonableness followed the Wednesbury standard: an order is struck down only if it is so irrational that no reasonable authority could have made it. In Modern Dental College v State of Madhya Pradesh (2016), the Supreme Court explained proportionality as a structured inquiry into whether a measure pursues a legitimate goal, is rationally connected to it, is necessary because no less restrictive alternative of equal efficacy exists, and strikes a balance between the right infringed and the benefit gained. Courts have applied proportionality chiefly where fundamental rights are restricted, while ordinary economic policy continues to attract deference. In Union of India v Hindustan Development Corporation (1993), the Court recognised legitimate expectation as a ground of review: it arises from a promise or a consistent past practice, is a procedural safeguard and not a substantive right to the benefit, and may yield to an overriding public interest if the authority gives reasons. In S N Mukherjee v Union of India (1990), it was held that administrative authorities must record reasons for decisions that affect rights, since reasons enable appeal and review, though a statute may exclude the requirement. On bias, Gullapalli Nowroji Reddy v Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (1959) held that a decision is vitiated where a person with a pecuniary or personal interest takes part, and the test applied is reasonable likelihood of bias, not proof of actual bias. The Court has also stressed that natural justice is not a straitjacket: its content varies with the statute, the subject matter and the urgency of the situation.

questions.question: The principal contribution of Maneka Gandhi, as described in the passage, is that

options.A: natural justice applies only where the statute expressly provides for notice and hearing, since courts cannot supply omitted procedure
options.B: Article 21 is attracted only when the State physically detains a person, because personal liberty means freedom from bodily restraint
options.C: a procedure prescribed by statute must itself be fair, just and reasonable, and is tested against Articles 14 and 19 as well
options.D: a procedure prescribed by a statute within legislative competence satisfies Article 21, whatever the fairness of its content

questions.explanation: Maneka Gandhi made the procedure under Article 21 subject to fairness and linked the Articles together.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A revives the narrow pre-Maneka reading in which any enacted procedure sufficed. Option B limits Article 21 to physical liberty, which the passage does not say. Option D contradicts the passage, which reads natural justice into statutory silence.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options are the pre-1978 position (procedure established by law, however unfair), so a student remembering A.K. Gopalan-style reasoning is lured.
questions.language_trick: 'must itself be' signals that fairness is a requirement of the procedure, not an add-on.

questions.question: A licensing authority has for ten years renewed a trader's licence after hearing him. It now cancels the licence without notice, citing a policy change that was never communicated. On the passage, the trader's best position is that

options.A: legitimate expectation is unavailable because it protects only express written promises and never a consistent course of past practice
options.B: he may invoke legitimate expectation to claim a hearing and reasons, although the authority may prevail on showing an overriding public interest
options.C: the cancellation is valid, because an authority's freedom to change policy leaves no room for any procedural safeguard in favour of existing licensees
options.D: he has acquired a substantive right to renewal on the same terms, which no later change of policy can defeat once a practice has run for a decade

questions.explanation: The passage says expectation arises from a promise or consistent past practice, is procedural, and yields to overriding public interest when reasons are given.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns a procedural safeguard into a substantive right. Option C ignores that past practice founds an expectation. Option D denies any procedural protection, contrary to the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Two options swing to the extremes (absolute right or no protection). The middle, qualified position is usually the right one in CLAT PG administrative-law items.
questions.language_trick: 'procedural safeguard and not a substantive right' is the key phrase.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: A measure passes the proportionality test if rationally connected to its goal, even where a less restrictive equally effective option exists
options.B: Wednesbury review interferes only with a decision so irrational that no reasonable authority, properly directing itself in law, could ever have reached it
options.C: The duty to record reasons for decisions affecting rights can be excluded by a statute that clearly says so, on the passage's account
options.D: A decision in which a person with a personal interest participates may be set aside on the basis of a reasonable likelihood of bias

questions.explanation: The necessity limb asks whether a less restrictive alternative of equal efficacy exists; if it does, the measure fails.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states the Wednesbury standard correctly. Option C follows the qualification in the S N Mukherjee discussion. Option D states the bias test as given.
questions.clat_trap: In a 'NOT consistent' stem the correct answer is the single wrong statement, and three true statements act as decoys.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT' in capitals reverses the task; the false statement omits the necessity limb.

questions.question: A member of a selection committee sits on it although his brother is one of the candidates. No evidence shows that he marked the brother higher than others. The selection is

options.A: valid unless the brother was ultimately selected, since bias is judged only through the outcome of the process
options.B: valid, because the challenger has not proved that the member actually favoured his brother in the marking
options.C: vitiated only if the member voted for the brother, since mere presence on the committee is immaterial
options.D: vitiated, because reasonable likelihood of bias is enough and actual prejudice need not be proved

questions.explanation: The Gullapalli test is reasonable likelihood of bias, not proof of actual bias.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A demands proof of actual bias. Option B ties bias to the result. Option C makes participation by voting a precondition.
questions.clat_trap: The lack of evidence of actual favouritism tempts students toward the 'valid' options.
questions.language_trick: 'reasonable likelihood' versus 'actual bias'.

questions.question: Consider the following statements: I. Legitimate expectation is a substantive right enforceable to compel the grant of the expected benefit. II. Authorities must record reasons for decisions that affect rights, though a statute may exclude this. III. The content of natural justice varies with the statute, the subject matter and the urgency. Which are consistent with the passage?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I and III only
options.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Statement I is wrong since legitimate expectation is only a procedural safeguard; statements II and III follow the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement I fails because the passage calls expectation a procedural safeguard.
questions.clat_trap: Statement I sounds like an extension of the doctrine, so students accept it, giving the 'all three' option.
questions.language_trick: 'substantive right' versus 'procedural safeguard'.

questions.question: A statute authorises immediate sealing of premises in a public-safety emergency but is silent on any prior hearing. On the passage, the best view is that

options.A: natural justice is wholly excluded, because the statute is silent on hearing and the situation is one of urgency and public safety
options.B: a full trial-type hearing before sealing is indispensable in every case, since silence implies it
options.C: a prior hearing may be curtailed or postponed because of urgency, but mere silence does not wholly exclude natural justice
options.D: the sealing is not open to review, because emergency powers are policy decisions beyond judicial scrutiny

questions.explanation: The passage reads natural justice into silence unless clear words exclude it, and says its content varies with urgency.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats silence as exclusion, contrary to the first part of the passage. Option B ignores the role of urgency. Option D claims non-justiciability, which the passage does not support.
questions.clat_trap: Two principles pull in opposite directions (silence implies natural justice; urgency relaxes it) and each wrong option picks one of them in an absolute form.
questions.language_trick: 'not wholly excluded' preserves a minimum content.

passages.title: Command, Rule, Norm and Jural Relation: Austin, Hart, Kelsen and Hohfeld
passages.passage: Analytical jurisprudence seeks to describe law as it is, apart from what it ought to be. John Austin defined law as a command of the sovereign backed by a sanction, the sovereign being a determinate person or body habitually obeyed by the bulk of society and not itself in the habit of obeying anyone. H L A Hart criticised this model: law includes power-conferring rules, such as those regulating contracts and wills, which cannot be reduced to orders backed by threats; and a legal system is better described as a union of primary rules, which impose duties, and secondary rules, which identify, change and adjudicate them. The rule of recognition, a secondary rule, supplies the criteria of validity, and Hart stressed the internal point of view of officials who accept the rule as a standard, rather than merely obey out of fear. Hans Kelsen's Pure Theory purges law of politics, ethics and sociology. For Kelsen, law is a hierarchy of norms in which each norm derives its validity from a higher norm, ending in the Grundnorm, which is presupposed and not enacted; the science of law deals with what ought to follow from stated conditions, not with what in fact happens. Wesley Hohfeld analysed legal relations into eight fundamental conceptions. A right in the strict sense correlates with a duty; a privilege correlates with a no-right; a power with a liability; and an immunity with a disability. Their jural opposites are, respectively, no-right, duty, disability and liability. Salmond defined a legal right as an interest protected by a rule of right, an interest the respect of which is a duty and the disregard of which is a wrong.

questions.question: Hart's objection to the command theory based on contracts and wills is that

options.A: law cannot be separated from morality, so Austin's definition leaves out the moral content of every rule
options.B: a sovereign who habitually obeys another person cannot make laws, so Austin's sovereign is only a fiction
options.C: sanctions play no part in any legal system, so a theory built on commands is wholly baseless
options.D: power-conferring rules cannot be explained as orders backed by threats

questions.explanation: Hart said rules enabling people to make contracts and wills confer powers and are not orders.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A attributes a natural-law objection to Hart. Option B is Austin's own premise, not Hart's criticism. Option C overstates Hart, who did not deny sanctions in all systems.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option is a true-sounding proposition about someone in the passage but not the objection asked for.
questions.language_trick: 'based on contracts and wills' narrows the objection to power-conferring rules.

questions.question: A, a landowner, is at liberty to walk on his own field, and B cannot demand that A stay off it. In Hohfeld's terms, A holds

options.A: a privilege, whose correlative is B's no-right
options.B: an immunity, whose correlative is B's disability to change A's position
options.C: a power, whose correlative is B's liability to have his legal position altered
options.D: a right in the strict sense, whose correlative is B's duty not to enter the field

questions.explanation: Liberty to do something with no claim in another to prevent it is a privilege, correlative to a no-right.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B would need B to owe A a duty. Option C requires ability to change legal relations. Option D requires inability of another to alter A's position.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'right' in everyday speech covers privilege, so the first wrong option is tempting.
questions.language_trick: 'at liberty' and 'cannot demand' indicate privilege and no-right.

questions.question: Under a statute the Registrar may cancel a society's registration. The society's legal position in relation to that Registrar's authority is best described as

options.A: a liability, which is the correlative of the Registrar's power
options.B: an immunity, since cancellation changes the society's legal position
options.C: a no-right, because the society cannot demand any protection against cancellation
options.D: a disability, because the society has no power to alter its own registration

questions.explanation: A power to alter another's legal position correlates with a liability in the person subject to it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B mixes up the correlative of an immunity. Option C is the correlative of a privilege. Option D states the opposite of liability.
questions.clat_trap: Four Hohfeldian terms are offered, three of which are real but attached to the wrong correlation.
questions.language_trick: The words 'in relation to that Registrar's authority' call for the correlative, not the opposite.

questions.question: In Kelsen's scheme the Grundnorm

options.A: is a moral principle of justice from which every valid norm must derive its content
options.B: is the first written constitution adopted by the founders of the State and ratified by the people through a formal procedure
options.C: is a presupposed ultimate norm that validates the hierarchy and is not itself enacted by any authority
options.D: is the sovereign's command whose breach attracts a sanction, enforced by a habit of obedience

questions.explanation: The passage says the Grundnorm is presupposed and not enacted, and validity flows down from it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats it as enacted text. Option B restores ethics, which the Pure Theory purges. Option D describes Austin.
questions.clat_trap: Students often equate Grundnorm with the constitution; the passage stresses 'presupposed'.
questions.language_trick: 'presupposed and not enacted'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): On Hart's account a rule of recognition can exist even where most ordinary citizens merely obey the law without accepting it as a standard. Reason (R): For Hart the internal point of view must be held by the officials who apply the rule, not necessarily by every citizen.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Hart required acceptance by officials; ordinary citizens might obey for other reasons.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R supplies precisely the condition that makes A possible.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'merely obey' triggers the Austinian picture of obedience, so students think A is false.
questions.language_trick: The contrast between officials and citizens.

questions.question: Which of the following pairings is NOT correct on the passage?

options.A: Salmond: a legal right is an interest protected by a rule of right
options.B: Hart: secondary rules identify, change and adjudicate the primary rules
options.C: Austin: the sovereign is habitually obeyed and is not in the habit of obeying anyone
options.D: Kelsen: a norm is valid only if it conforms to the moral standards of the community

questions.explanation: Kelsen purged law of ethics; validity comes from a higher norm, not from morality.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option B and Option C reproduce the passage accurately.
questions.clat_trap: A negatively framed stem with three true pairings requires hunting the one false pairing.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT correct' inverts the task.

passages.title: Treaties, Custom and Obligations of States: From Vienna to the Climate Advisory Opinion
passages.passage: Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice lists treaties, international custom, general principles of law recognised by civilised nations and, as subsidiary means, judicial decisions and the teachings of publicists. Treaty law is largely codified in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969. Article 26 states pacta sunt servanda: a treaty in force binds the parties and must be performed in good faith. Article 27 provides that a party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform a treaty. A State may formulate a reservation on ratifying unless the treaty prohibits it or the reservation is incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose. A treaty is void if it conflicts with a peremptory norm of general international law (jus cogens), from which no derogation is permitted; a fundamental change of circumstances may be invoked to terminate a treaty only in narrow cases and not where the change results from the invoking party's own breach. A State that persistently objects to an emerging customary rule during its formation is not bound by it, though the objection does not avail against jus cogens. Obligations erga omnes, recognised in Barcelona Traction (1970), are owed to the international community as a whole, so every State has a legal interest in their protection. In July 2025 the ICJ delivered an advisory opinion on the obligations of States in respect of climate change, indicating that States have duties under treaties and customary law to protect the climate system and that breach may amount to an internationally wrongful act (the detailed findings should be verified). Advisory opinions are not binding in themselves. In India, Article 51(c) directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, Article 253 enables Parliament to legislate to give effect to them, and the Supreme Court has held that international norms not in conflict with municipal law may be read into domestic law, as in Vishaka (1997), while a conflicting statute prevails in Indian courts (Gramophone Company, 1984).

questions.question: A State pleads that its constitution forbids it from performing a treaty it ratified. On the passage, the plea

options.A: succeeds only if the other parties had notice of the domestic provision at the time of ratification
options.B: succeeds, since a State's constitution is supreme over every obligation it accepts through treaty
options.C: fails, because a party may not rely on its internal law to justify non-performance of a treaty
options.D: succeeds, where the constitutional provision was adopted before the State ratified the treaty in question

questions.explanation: Article 27 as described bars reliance on internal law; the passage mentions no exception for earlier provisions or notice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adds a timing exception not in the passage. Option B asserts constitutional supremacy over treaty obligations at the international level. Option D invents a notice condition.
questions.clat_trap: The options sound like plausible nuances; the question is answered from the passage's flat rule.
questions.language_trick: 'may not invoke' is categorical.

questions.question: State A consistently objected, while a customary rule on maritime interception was forming, to its crystallisation. The rule is later claimed against A. On the passage, A

options.A: is not bound, since an objection prevails against every rule, including peremptory norms
options.B: is bound, since a custom once crystallised binds every State regardless of any earlier and consistent objection it made
options.C: is bound, unless it has also entered a written reservation to a treaty on the same subject
options.D: is not bound as a persistent objector, unless the rule has become jus cogens

questions.explanation: The passage preserves the persistent-objector exception but not against jus cogens.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the exception. Option B extends it to jus cogens. Option C confuses custom with treaty reservations.
questions.clat_trap: The qualifier 'unless jus cogens' is easy to drop; two options each drop one half of the rule.
questions.language_trick: 'during its formation' fixes the timing of the objection.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: A State cannot terminate a treaty on changed circumstances where its own breach produced the change in circumstances
options.B: The climate advisory opinion is a binding judgment creating enforceable liability against named States
options.C: Obligations erga omnes give every State a legal interest in their protection
options.D: A reservation incompatible with the object and purpose of a treaty is not permissible

questions.explanation: The passage states that advisory opinions are not binding in themselves.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D reflect the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Ready familiarity with the ICJ makes the statement sound plausible; contentious jurisdiction is confused with advisory jurisdiction.
questions.language_trick: 'binding judgment' against 'advisory opinion'.

questions.question: No Indian statute covers a field, and India has ratified a convention that does. On the passage, the Supreme Court may

options.A: read the convention's norms into fundamental rights to fill the gap, as in Vishaka
options.B: treat the convention as automatically enforceable law with no reading or legislation, by force of Article 51(c) alone
options.C: decline, because only Parliament acting under Article 253 can ever give effect to a convention
options.D: do so even where a statute directly conflicts, since treaty norms outrank every statute

questions.explanation: International norms not in conflict with municipal law may be read in, as in Vishaka.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B denies judicial role contrary to Vishaka. Option C ignores that a conflicting statute prevails. Option D treats Article 51(c) as a self-executing rule.
questions.clat_trap: Article 51(c) is a Directive Principle, and students over-read it.
questions.language_trick: 'no Indian statute covers' means there is no conflict.

questions.question: Consider the following statements: I. A treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm is void. II. A State may invoke its internal law under Article 27 if the provision is constitutional. III. Erga omnes obligations give every State a legal interest in their protection. Which are consistent with the passage?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I and III only
options.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Statements I and III follow the passage; statement II reverses Article 27.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II contradicts the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Statement II dresses a constitutional claim as a legitimate exception.
questions.language_trick: 'if the provision is constitutional' is an invented exception.

questions.question: An Indian statute conflicts with a treaty norm that Parliament has never legislated to implement. On the passage, in Indian courts

options.A: the Court must strike down the statute, since international law forms part of the basic structure
options.B: the statute prevails, though the State may still incur international responsibility for the breach
options.C: the statute is void, because the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties overrides domestic enactments and domestic courts must give it priority
options.D: the treaty norm prevails, because Article 51(c) makes it superior to every statute enacted by Parliament in India

questions.explanation: Gramophone Company holds that a conflicting statute prevails; Article 27 means the State's responsibility continues internationally.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overrates Article 51(c). Option C treats the Vienna Convention as binding on domestic courts. Option D invents a basic-structure link.
questions.clat_trap: Domestic and international planes are mixed in the options. The correct answer separates them.
questions.language_trick: 'in Indian courts' limits the plane of the answer.

passages.title: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019: Consumer, Jurisdiction and Product Liability
passages.passage: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 Act and created the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), with powers to regulate matters affecting consumers collectively, investigate, order recall of goods and refund of prices, and penalise misleading advertisements. A consumer is a person who buys goods or hires services for consideration, but not one who obtains them for resale or for a commercial purpose; commercial purpose does not include use of goods bought and used exclusively for earning a livelihood by self-employment. In Laxmi Engineering Works v P S G Industrial Institute (1995), the Supreme Court held that whether a purchase is for a commercial purpose depends on the dominant purpose and that a buyer using machinery to earn a livelihood by self-employment is within the Act. In Shrikant G Mantri v Punjab National Bank (2022), it held that a person who has taken a loan for a commercial activity is not a consumer in respect of the bank's service. Pecuniary jurisdiction is set by the value of the consideration paid; under the 2021 Rules the District Commission hears claims up to fifty lakh rupees, the State Commission from fifty lakh to two crore rupees, and the National Commission above two crore rupees. The chapter on product liability makes the manufacturer, the service provider and the product seller liable for harm caused by a defective product or deficient service, each on specified grounds. A complaint must be filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action arises, though the Commission may condone delay for sufficient cause. The Act also introduced provisions on unfair contracts, e-commerce and mediation.

questions.question: A buyer pays Rs 1.2 crore for goods and claims Rs 3 crore as compensation for defects. The proper forum is

options.A: the National Commission, because the compensation claimed exceeds two crore rupees
options.B: the National Commission, because the price and the compensation taken together exceed two crore rupees
options.C: the State Commission, because jurisdiction turns on the consideration paid and not on the compensation claimed
options.D: the District Commission, because the goods were bought for a sum smaller than the compensation sought

questions.explanation: Pecuniary jurisdiction follows the consideration paid; Rs 1.2 crore falls between fifty lakh and two crore.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A uses the compensation claimed, which is not the test. Option B compares price with compensation, which is irrelevant. Option D adds the two figures, which the rules do not do.
questions.clat_trap: The large claim figure is a decoy; the 2019 Act changed the test from claim value to consideration paid.
questions.language_trick: 'consideration paid' versus 'claimed'.

questions.question: A tailor buys a sewing machine exclusively to earn his livelihood from self-employment. On the passage, he is

options.A: a consumer, since goods used exclusively to earn a livelihood by self-employment are not for a commercial purpose
options.B: a consumer only if the machine's price is below the pecuniary limit of the District Commission
options.C: not a consumer, since the machine was bought for business and not for household consumption
options.D: not a consumer, since any use of machinery in an income-generating activity is a commercial purpose that takes the buyer outside the Act

questions.explanation: The exception for self-employed livelihood applies, in line with Laxmi Engineering Works.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the livelihood exception. Option C restricts consumers to household use. Option D makes status turn on price instead of purpose.
questions.clat_trap: 'business' and 'income-generating' tempt students to apply a blanket commercial-purpose exclusion.
questions.language_trick: 'exclusively' makes the exception apply.

questions.question: A company borrows from a bank to expand its manufacturing business and alleges deficiency in the bank's processing of the loan. On the passage, the company is

options.A: a consumer, since banking is a service hired for consideration, whatever may be the purpose for which the loan is taken
options.B: not a consumer only if the loan exceeds the fifty lakh limit of the District Commission
options.C: not a consumer in respect of that service, since a loan taken for commercial activity is outside the Act
options.D: a consumer, because the dominant purpose test applies to goods and not to services

questions.explanation: Shrikant Mantri holds that a loan taken for commercial activity does not make the borrower a consumer.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the commercial-purpose exclusion. Option B confines dominant purpose to goods without basis. Option D confuses jurisdiction with status.
questions.clat_trap: Banking is a classic consumer service, so the exclusion is easy to forget.
questions.language_trick: 'commercial activity' triggers the exclusion.

questions.question: A cause of action arose on 1 January 2023, and the complaint is filed on 15 March 2025 with no explanation for the delay. The complaint is

options.A: barred absolutely, because the Commission has no power whatsoever to condone any delay under any circumstances
options.B: dismissed as time-barred, since two years have run and no sufficient cause for delay is shown
options.C: maintainable, because the two years run from the date of the last correspondence exchanged between the parties
options.D: maintainable, because delay beyond two years is automatically condoned in the case of consumers

questions.explanation: The two-year period runs from the cause of action; condonation needs sufficient cause.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A shifts the starting point. Option C makes condonation automatic. Option D denies the Commission's power of condonation.
questions.clat_trap: 'automatically' and 'absolutely' are the over-statements that wrap the correct, qualified position.
questions.language_trick: 'sufficient cause' is the condition.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Only the manufacturer can be held liable under the product liability chapter when a defective product causes harm. Reason (R): The Act makes the manufacturer, the service provider and the product seller liable, each on specified grounds.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because the product seller and the service provider are also covered; R is true.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R itself contradicts A.
questions.clat_trap: A looks natural since manufacturers are the usual defendants; the word 'only' is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'Only' in the assertion.

questions.question: The 'dominant purpose' test adopted in Laxmi Engineering Works implies that

options.A: only a purchase of consumer goods for the household can ever qualify, since machinery is always bought commercially
options.B: the buyer's own description of the purpose in the complaint is conclusive and the Commission cannot examine it
options.C: any purchase from which the buyer later makes a profit is outside the Act, whatever the main reason for buying
options.D: a purchase made mainly for personal use or self-employed livelihood is not turned into a commercial one by some incidental profit

questions.explanation: The test looks to the main purpose of the transaction. Incidental profit does not make a purchase commercial, and the livelihood-by-self-employment exception shows the same approach.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores 'dominant' and treats any profit as disqualifying. Option B reads the self-employment exception out of the Act with an absolute 'always'. Option C makes the buyer's label conclusive, which the passage does not support.
questions.clat_trap: Words like 'any', 'only' and 'always' make the wrong options sound firm, while the correct option is hedged with 'mainly' and 'incidental'.
questions.language_trick: 'dominant' signals a weighing of purposes; 'exclusively' in the statutory exception is a stricter word that students merge with it.

passages.title: LARR Act, 2013: Consent, Compensation and the Lapse Controversy
passages.passage: The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (the LARR Act) replaced the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. It requires a Social Impact Assessment for most acquisitions, the consent of at least eighty per cent of affected families for private projects and seventy per cent for public-private partnership projects, compensation based on market value multiplied by a factor of up to two in rural areas, and a solatium of one hundred per cent of the compensation. The urgency clause in section 17 permits dispensing with certain procedural steps for defence, security or emergency needs. Section 24(2) deals with acquisitions begun under the 1894 Act: where an award was made five years or more before the commencement of the 2013 Act and physical possession has not been taken or compensation has not been paid, the proceedings are deemed to lapse. In Pune Municipal Corporation v Harakchand Misirimal Solanki (2014), it was held that compensation is paid only if tendered to the landowner or deposited in court and that a deposit in the treasury does not suffice, so that lapse follows if either condition fails. A five-judge Bench in Indore Development Authority v Manoharlal (2020) overruled that view. It held that lapse occurs only where the authority has failed both to take possession and to pay compensation, the word 'or' being read as 'nor'; that the duty to pay is discharged by tendering the amount, and a landowner who refuses to accept it cannot claim lapse for want of deposit in court; and that the period during which the process was stayed by court order is excluded from the five-year count. It also held that the section does not revive stale claims. Acquisition also engages Article 300A, under which no person may be deprived of property except by authority of law.

questions.question: For a public-private partnership project, the LARR Act requires the consent of

options.A: at least seventy per cent of the affected families
options.B: no one, because a public-private partnership project is by its nature a public purpose acquisition
options.C: only the landowners, and not other affected families who depend on the land
options.D: at least eighty per cent of the affected families, as in the case of private projects

questions.explanation: The passage fixes seventy per cent for PPP projects and eighty per cent for private ones.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B uses the private-project figure. Option C narrows the class without basis. Option D claims no consent is needed.
questions.clat_trap: Two close percentages are the whole trap; mixing them is a classic slip.
questions.language_trick: 'public-private' versus 'private'.

questions.question: An award was made in 2005 and the authority took physical possession in 2006. Compensation was never paid and the owners never approached any court. After the 2013 Act commenced, the proceedings

options.A: do not lapse, because the owners failed to move the Court within five years of the award
options.B: lapse, because an award made five years or more before the Act is sufficient by itself
options.C: do not lapse, because possession was taken and lapse requires failure on both counts
options.D: lapse, because compensation was not paid even though possession was taken

questions.explanation: After Indore Development Authority, lapse needs both non-possession and non-payment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A follows the overruled Pune Municipal approach. Option B drops the other conditions. Option D invents a condition about approaching the Court.
questions.clat_trap: The older decision gave an 'either' test; the passage's later decision gave 'both'.
questions.language_trick: 'or' read as 'nor'.

questions.question: Possession was not taken, but compensation was tendered to the owner, who refused it, and the authority did not deposit it in court. The owner claims lapse. On the passage, the claim

options.A: fails only if the authority also deposited the amount in the treasury, since tender is valid on that condition
options.B: fails, because tender discharges the duty to pay and a refusing owner cannot claim lapse for want of deposit
options.C: succeeds, since failure to take possession alone is enough, the word 'or' being read disjunctively
options.D: succeeds, because the authority did not deposit the refused amount in court, so payment is incomplete

questions.explanation: Payment is satisfied by tender; since compensation is treated as paid, both defaults are not present.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A requires deposit after refusal, which the Bench did not. Option C adopts the overruled disjunctive reading. Option D reintroduces treasury deposit as a condition, which the passage rejects.
questions.clat_trap: The facts include both a default (possession) and a deceptive one (non-deposit); the pair test makes the claim fail.
questions.language_trick: 'tender' versus 'deposit'.

questions.question: A court stays the acquisition process for three years during the five-year period. In counting the five years, the stay period is

options.A: used to restart the five-year period from the date of vacation of the stay
options.B: included, since the authority could have sought vacation of the stay
options.C: deducted from the period so as to shorten it in favour of the owner
options.D: excluded from the count

questions.explanation: The Bench excluded the stayed period from the five-year count.

questions.question: Consider the following statements: I. Pune Municipal held that deposit in the treasury does not amount to payment and that lapse follows if either condition fails. II. Indore Development Authority read 'or' as 'nor', so lapse requires both failures. III. Section 24(2) revives stale claims even where owners did not move earlier. Which are consistent with the passage?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I and III only
options.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Statements I and II reproduce the passage; statement III contradicts the Bench's holding that stale claims are not revived.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement III contradicts the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Statement III sounds pro-owner and fits the remedial tone of the Act.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the effect of Article 300A as stated in the passage?

options.A: It confers a fundamental right to market-value compensation in every acquisition under Part III
options.B: It applies only where possession has been taken, because initiation of proceedings deprives no one of property
options.C: A deprivation of property must be authorised by law, so an acquisition without statutory authority is unconstitutional even for a public purpose
options.D: It bars acquisition for private projects altogether, even where the consent of the affected families has been obtained and rehabilitation is provided

questions.explanation: Article 300A requires authority of law for deprivation of property.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns it into a fundamental right to compensation. Option B bars acquisition for private projects, which the LARR Act permits with consent. Option D adds a possession condition not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Options mix Part III (fundamental rights) with Article 300A, which stands outside it after the 44th Amendment.
questions.language_trick: 'by authority of law' is the full content in the passage.
